title: Why one big task fails and six small ones don't
description: What actually goes wrong when an agent is handed one large instruction, and why the same work broken into steps survives contact with reality.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a single large agent task produces failures that are hard to locate
Identify the point in a large task's transcript where verification would have caught the problem earlier

contentSections.title: One prompt, forty minutes, one enormous diff

contentSections.body: You tell an agent: "migrate our session-based auth to JWTs." It runs for forty minutes, touches nineteen files, and comes back with: "Done — migrated auth to JWTs, updated the login flow, added token refresh, and updated the tests." You open the diff. The login route issues a token. Nothing validates it on protected routes — they still check `req.session.user`. The refresh endpoint exists and calls a function that was never defined. Three test files were edited; two of them now test nothing, because the assertions were commented out rather than fixed. You did not find any of this by reading the summary. You found it by reading nineteen files end to end, forty minutes after the agent told you it was done.

None of those problems are exotic. An unvalidated protected route, a call to an undefined function, a disabled test — each one, in isolation, is a five-minute fix. What made this expensive wasn't the difficulty of any single defect; it was that all four arrived bundled into one unbroken run with no point where you could have caught the first one before the agent built on top of it. The undefined refresh function and the still-session-based route checks aren't independent mistakes — the agent kept going after each one, writing code that assumed the earlier step had worked.

A task description like "migrate auth to JWTs" names an outcome, not a sequence of checkable moves. Handed a task shaped like that, an agent has to invent its own decomposition on the fly, mid-run, with no chance for you to look at the plan before it starts executing it — and it has no way to tell you "I'm not sure the login route change was applied everywhere it needed to be" partway through, because nothing in a single unbroken instruction asks it to pause and report. The failure isn't that the agent is bad at JWTs. It's that the task, as given, contained no place to stop.

contentSections.scenario: Same task, same agent, but this time the transcript shows the agent working through six separate instructions, one at a time, each one starting only after you replied "looks right, go on" to the last: (1) add JWT issuance to login, (2) add a middleware that validates a JWT on protected routes, (3) point protected routes at the new middleware, (4) add token refresh, (5) update tests to match, (6) remove the old session code. The same eventual defects — an undefined refresh function, routes not repointed — still would have been possible. But they showed up differently.
contentSections.question: What actually changed between the one-shot version and the six-step version?

options.label: The agent became more careful because it knew it was being watched more closely
Each step produced a small, specific point where a defect became visible before the next step could build on it
Nothing changed — six small prompts and one large prompt ask for identical work and carry identical risk

feedback.checkpoint: Right. Step 3 ("point protected routes at the new middleware") is where you'd have noticed the routes still checking `req.session.user` — one diff, one specific thing to check, before step 4 built a refresh flow on top of an auth check that wasn't actually wired up yet. The defect is the same; where it becomes visible is not.
feedback.more-careful: There's no mechanism here that would make the same underlying model more careful — same model, same instructions in aggregate, same eventual code. What changed is structural: the work got cut at points where a person could look before the next piece was built.
feedback.nothing-changed: The total scope of work is the same, but risk isn't just a function of scope — it's a function of how much can go wrong *before anyone looks*. One 40-minute run with zero checkpoints and six 6-minute runs with five checkpoints between them are not the same risk, even producing an identical final diff.

contentSections.mechanism: A step boundary is a place where a person's judgment can enter before more work is built on an assumption. The value of decomposition isn't that smaller tasks are individually easier — a lot of the six steps above are exactly as hard as the corresponding fragment of the big task. The value is that each boundary is a chance to catch a wrong assumption while it's cheap: one step's output, not four steps' worth of code built on top of it.

contentSections.body: The cost of a mistake in agent work is set less by how hard the mistake is to fix and more by how much got built on top of it before anyone looked.

contentSections.title: What makes a step small enough

contentSections.body:
"Smaller" isn't the actual target — a task chopped into twenty trivial, arbitrary fragments is not obviously safer than six well-chosen ones, and can be worse, because each fragment now needs its own review overhead with no more insight per step. The property that matters is whether a step's result can be checked on its own, against something concrete, without needing to trust the step's own narration of what it did. "Add JWT issuance to login" can be checked: call the login endpoint, look at the response, confirm a token is actually there and actually well-formed. "Migrate auth to JWTs" cannot be checked in one look — checking it means re-deriving the whole six-step breakdown yourself, after the fact, from a diff, which is strictly more work than deciding the breakdown before anything ran.

This is the one habit this whole module builds toward: before an agent starts multi-step work, decide what the steps are and what "this step worked" will concretely look like for each one — not because more steps are inherently better, but because a step without a concrete check attached is a step where a wrong assumption gets to travel forward undetected.

contentSections.scenario: A learner is about to hand an agent a decomposition for "add CSV export to the reports page." Four candidate steps.
contentSections.question: Select every step below that is small enough to check on its own, without having to re-derive the whole feature from the diff.

items.label: "Add a /reports/export endpoint that returns the current report's rows as CSV, tested against one report with a known row count"
"Wire up CSV export"
"Add an 'Export CSV' button to the reports page that calls the new endpoint and triggers a file download"
"Make sure export works well"

explanation.s1: Checkable: hit the endpoint, count the rows in the response, compare to the known count. A pass/fail question with a concrete answer.
explanation.s2: This is the whole feature restated, not a step of it — there's no way to look at one piece of output and say whether "wired up" happened; you'd have to test the entire feature end to end to know.
explanation.s3: Checkable: click the button, confirm a download starts, open the file. Specific and concrete, independent of whether the endpoint step is perfect.
explanation.s4: "Works well" names no observable fact — it's a feeling about the feature, not a condition you can check the diff against. It's the kind of step description that lets a defect hide behind an agent's own confident summary.

contentSections.body: A step earns its size not by being short, but by having something concrete you could check it against without re-reading the whole diff.

title: A step is done when something checkable is true
description: Turning a vague step description into a verification condition — a concrete, observable fact you can check without trusting the agent's own account of what it did.

learningObjectives.text: Convert a vague step description into a verification condition that names a specific observable fact
Distinguish a verification condition from a restatement of the step itself

contentSections.title: "Add validation" is not a finish line

contentSections.body: The step reads: "add validation to the signup form." The agent reports: "Added validation to the signup form." Both sentences are true and neither one tells you whether an empty email gets rejected, whether a password under eight characters gets rejected, or whether the validation runs client-side only and a raw POST to the endpoint sails straight through. "Add validation" describes an intention, not a state of the world you could go check. The agent's own report of having done it is exactly as unverifiable as the instruction that produced it — restating the task in the past tense is not evidence the task happened.

A verification condition is a specific, observable fact that is either true or false about the system after a step runs — something you (or a test) can check directly, without relying on the agent's narration. "Add validation" has no verification condition attached to it; "a POST to /signup with an empty email field returns a 400 and no user row is created" does. The difference isn't formality — it's that the second sentence names an input, an expected output, and a way to check it happened, all in one place. You can run that exact request yourself and get a yes or no answer that doesn't depend on trusting anyone's summary.

Writing the verification condition before the step runs — not after, as a way of checking the agent's work retroactively — does something extra: it forces the ambiguity in the original instruction to surface early. "Add validation" leaves open which fields, which rules, client-side or server-side, and what happens on failure. Trying to write "this step is done when ___" forces you to answer those questions yourself, before the agent guesses at an answer and builds a whole implementation around its guess.

contentSections.problem: Turn this step into a verification condition: "Add rate limiting to the login endpoint."

steps.label: Name the specific behavior the step is actually supposed to produce
steps.work: Not "rate limiting exists" in the abstract — the concrete behavior: after some number of failed attempts from the same source in some window, further attempts should be rejected rather than processed.
steps.why: The step description names a feature by category ("rate limiting") rather than a behavior. Categories don't have pass/fail states; specific behaviors do.

steps.label: Pick concrete numbers rather than leaving them implicit
steps.work: "5 failed attempts from the same IP within 60 seconds" — a specific threshold and window, chosen and written down, not left for the agent to invent silently.
steps.why: If you don't pick the threshold, the agent will — and you'll find out what it picked by testing the finished code, which is exactly the after-the-fact discovery this module is trying to avoid.

steps.label: State the observable outcome for both the pass and fail input
steps.work: "A 6th failed login attempt from the same IP within 60 seconds returns 429, not 401. A 6th attempt from a *different* IP within the same window still returns 401 normally."
steps.why: Testing only the blocked case can pass even if the limiter is far too aggressive (blocking everyone) — checking the unaffected case too confirms the limit is scoped to what you actually specified, not just present.

faded.problem: Turn this step into a verification condition: "Add pagination to the /orders endpoint."

blanks.prompt: Name the specific behavior, not the feature category.
blanks.answer: Requesting a page of orders returns a bounded number of results per request, with a way to request the next page.
accept: bounded results per page with a next-page mechanism
blanks.why: "Pagination" names a category of feature; a verification condition needs the actual shape of the request/response contract.

blanks.prompt: Pick concrete numbers and name them.
blanks.answer: e.g. page size of 20 by default, a `?page=` or cursor parameter for the next page.
accept: specific page size and paging parameter
blanks.why: An unstated default page size is exactly the kind of gap an agent will fill in silently, and differently than you'd have picked.

blanks.prompt: State the observable outcome you'd actually go check.
blanks.answer: `GET /orders?page=1` with 45 total orders returns exactly 20 results and a marker indicating a page 2 exists; `GET /orders?page=3` returns the remaining 5 and a marker indicating no further page.
accept: a specific request against a known total returns the expected count and a correct next-page indicator
blanks.why: This is checkable against a fixture with a known order count, in one look, without needing to trust a summary of what the pagination code does.

contentSections.procedure: For any step: name the specific behavior (not the feature category), pick and write down the concrete numbers the instruction left implicit, then state an observable outcome for both a passing and a failing input.

contentSections.body: If you can't write "this step is done when ___" with a specific, checkable fact in the blank, the step isn't specified yet — the agent is about to specify it for you.

contentSections.title: When the condition is a restatement, not a check

contentSections.body:
The most common failure in writing verification conditions isn't skipping them — it's writing one that just restates the step in slightly more words, which feels like progress but checks nothing new. "Done when the endpoint returns paginated results" for a pagination step is the same sentence with a different verb tense; it still doesn't say what a passing test would actually assert. A real verification condition names an input you didn't have to invent (a known fixture, a known count, a known bad value) and an output you can compare against a specific expectation, not just "the right kind of thing happens."

A second, quieter failure: writing a verification condition that's technically checkable but checks the wrong thing — confirming the code *runs* without confirming it does what was actually asked. "The endpoint returns a 200" is checkable and nearly worthless on its own if the actual requirement was about *which* rows come back, not whether a response arrives at all. The condition has to target the part of the requirement that's actually at risk of being wrong, not the part that was never really in question.

contentSections.code:
Step: "Add a discount code field to checkout — codes over 20% off require manager approval before applying."
Verification condition written: "Done when checkout accepts a discount code and applies the discount."
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong with this verification condition?

options.label: It restates the feature rather than checking the one specific rule (the 20% manager-approval threshold) that's actually at risk of being implemented wrong
Nothing — it correctly describes what the step should do
It's too specific and over-constrains the implementation

feedback.restates: Right. A generic discount code applying is the easy, low-risk part — an agent will very likely get that right without help. The part of this step that's actually specified enough to get wrong is the 20%-and-up manager-approval rule, and the written condition doesn't mention it at all. If that rule silently doesn't get implemented, this verification condition still passes.
feedback.fine: It would pass whether or not the approval rule exists, which is exactly the problem — a condition that can't tell the difference between the correct implementation and the one specific way this feature is likely to go wrong isn't checking the thing that matters.
feedback.too-specific: The opposite problem, if anything — it's under-specific. It doesn't mention the 20% threshold, the manager-approval flow, or what happens to a code below the threshold, all of which are the actual content of the instruction.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Good verification conditions target the part of a requirement most likely to be silently dropped or guessed wrong — here, a numeric threshold with a conditional behavior attached. A revised condition: "a code for 15% off applies immediately with no approval step; a code for 25% off is held in a pending state and does not apply the discount until a manager approves it." That names both branches of the actual rule, not just the feature's existence.

contentSections.body: Aim a verification condition at the specific part of the instruction most likely to get quietly dropped or guessed wrong — not at whether the feature exists at all.

contentSections.title: Do it once yourself first

contentSections.body:
A checkable condition tells the agent when a step is done. It does not tell the agent what good looks like. "Write a good summary" cannot be checked, by you or by the agent, because neither of you has written down what good means.

The fix is old and plain. Do a small version of the task yourself, once, or find one that already exists. Keep it. That one example is worth more than a page of instructions, because the agent can compare its work against it and so can you.

An example alone is not enough. Add the short list of things it must contain, written as yes or no checks. Then add one bad example and say what is wrong with it. The bad one marks the edge of the task.

The low-energy version is small. One real example, three yes or no checks, one bad example in two lines. A spreadsheet row per check is fine.

contentSections.intro: Task: "Turn a customer complaint email into a ticket for the support team." Build the standard of good, one decision at a time, before any agent sees the task.

fields.prompt: What do you give the agent as the picture of good?

options.label: The words "write a good ticket"
One real ticket you wrote yourself, with the parts it must contain marked
A long description of your team's values

feedback.real-example: Right. The agent and you can both compare a result against it. Doing it once yourself is also how you find out what the hard part of the task really is.
feedback.words: "Good" names no observable fact. The agent will supply its own idea of good, and you will only learn what it chose by reading the result.
feedback.values: Values are real, but they cannot be checked against a result. A real example carries the same preferences in a form you can compare.

fields.prompt: How do you say what done means?

options.label: "The customer should be happy with it"
Three yes or no checks: names the product, states what the customer wants, quotes any error text
"It should look professional"

feedback.three-checks: Right. Each one can be answered yes or no in seconds, by you or by a second pass of the agent.
feedback.happy: You cannot check this against a ticket, because the customer has not read the ticket yet. It is a hope, not a condition.
feedback.professional: Looks professional is a feeling. Two people will disagree about it, and so will two runs of the same agent.

fields.prompt: What else do you show it?

options.label: One bad ticket and a line on what is wrong with it
Nothing more, one good example is enough
Ten more good tickets

feedback.bad-example: Right. The bad example marks where good stops, which the good example cannot do on its own. For instance, a ticket that is polite but never says what the customer wants.
feedback.nothing: A good example shows the middle of the task. It does not show the edge, which is where agents tend to wander.
feedback.more-good: More of the same adds little. One counter-example adds more information than ten more good ones.

contentSections.synthesis: One real example, three yes or no checks and one bad example. That is the whole standard. It takes about fifteen minutes to write, and it is the only part of the job the agent cannot do for you.

contentSections.body: "Do a great job" cannot be checked. A real example, three yes or no checks and one bad example can.

title: Ordering steps so a failure stops cheaply
description: Choosing which step goes first — not by what's easiest, but by what makes a wrong assumption visible before anything expensive is built on it.

learningObjectives.text: Order a set of steps so that cheap, information-revealing work happens before expensive or hard-to-reverse work
Identify when a step's position in the sequence, not its content, is the actual defect in a plan

contentSections.title: Same six steps, two different orders

contentSections.body: Task: replace a deprecated payment SDK across the codebase, twelve call sites. Plan A: rip out the old SDK everywhere first, then wire in the new one, then test. Plan B: pick the one call site that's easiest to fully test in isolation, migrate just that one, verify it end to end against the sandbox API, and only then touch the other eleven. Plan A finishes faster if nothing goes wrong. Plan B finds out, on call site one of twelve, that the new SDK's refund method has a different signature than the agent assumed — before that wrong assumption got copied into the other eleven call sites.

Step order isn't just about dependencies in the obvious sense — step 2 needing step 1's output. It's about where in the sequence a wrong assumption gets exposed, and how much work sits on top of it by the time that happens. Two plans can touch the exact same set of files and differ only in order, and one of them is far riskier, because it defers the one step that would have revealed a bad assumption until after that assumption has already been baked into eleven other places.

The general shape: do the step that's cheapest to verify and most likely to reveal a wrong assumption *first*, even if it isn't the most natural starting point. A single fully-tested call site is cheap to check and, if the SDK assumption was wrong, cheap to redo. The same wrong assumption discovered after twelve call sites are all migrated means twelve places to fix, not one — the mistake didn't get more likely, it just got twelve times more expensive to unwind.

contentSections.question: Task: add a new required field to a shared `Order` database table, used by three internal services (checkout, fulfillment, billing) that each read and write it independently. Put these four steps in the order that surfaces a wrong assumption cheapest.
steps: Add the column as nullable, with no service yet reading or writing it
Update checkout to write the new field on order creation, and verify with one real order that the value lands correctly
Update fulfillment and billing to read the new field, and verify each against the order checkout just created
Make the column non-nullable and add a default for existing rows, once all three services are confirmed writing/reading it correctly
contentSections.explanation: Adding the column nullable first is the cheapest possible move — it changes nothing about how any service behaves yet, so if the schema itself needs adjusting (wrong type, wrong name), nothing downstream has to be redone. Verifying checkout's write against one real order next confirms the column actually receives correct data before two more services are built assuming it does. Fulfillment and billing reading that same real order next tests the *consuming* side against data that's already confirmed correct, rather than against a guess. Only after all three services are proven working does the column become non-nullable — a change that's genuinely hard to reverse once other code depends on the column always having a value, so it's held until last, after every softer, reversible step has already surfaced whatever was going to go wrong.

contentSections.body: Order steps by where a wrong assumption gets found, not by which step feels like the natural place to begin.

contentSections.title: Reversible first, destructive last

contentSections.body:
A second ordering rule, independent of dependency and cost-of-verification: put reversible steps before irreversible ones, whenever the task offers a choice. Reading a config, writing a new file, adding a nullable column — these can be undone or ignored if something downstream turns out wrong. Deleting a table, force-pushing a rewritten history, rotating a credential that other running services still hold a copy of — these cannot be casually undone, and a mistake discovered after one of them has already run is a mistake you're now recovering from, not one you're preventing.

When a plan has exactly one destructive step among several safe ones, that step's position is not a detail — it's the single highest-leverage thing to get right in the whole plan. Put every step that could reveal "actually, this whole approach was wrong" before the destructive one, even if the destructive one would be more natural to do earlier by pure task logic. The five extra minutes it costs to defer a deletion is cheap compared to what it costs to have deleted the wrong thing.

contentSections.scenario: Task: "Consolidate three duplicate user-preferences tables into one, then drop the old two." A proposed step order: (1) drop `preferences_v1` and `preferences_v2`, (2) create the new unified table, (3) backfill from... wait, there's nothing left to backfill from.
contentSections.question: What's the actual defect in this plan?

options.label: The irreversible step (dropping the old tables) was placed before the step that depends on the old tables still existing
Dropping two tables in one step instead of two separate steps
The plan doesn't specify which columns to keep

feedback.order-defect: Right, and notice this isn't even subtle once named — the backfill step needs data from the old tables, and the old tables are already gone by the time it runs. This is what makes ordering worth checking explicitly rather than trusting a plan reads correctly: an agent generating steps in a plausible-sounding order can produce exactly this kind of self-defeating sequence without anything about any individual step looking wrong.
feedback.batching: Batching the two drops together isn't what breaks this plan — dropping them separately in the same wrong position would fail identically. The problem is where the destructive step sits relative to the step that needs its target to still exist.
feedback.missing-spec: A real gap in a more detailed version of this plan, but it's not what makes this specific four-step sequence fail — the sequence fails even with perfectly specified columns, because of what step 1 destroys before step 3 needs it.

contentSections.concept: Checking step order isn't just about dependencies that produce an error message (a function called before it's defined) — it includes dependencies on data or state that a later step needs and an earlier step just destroyed. The check: for every destructive step, does anything later in the plan need what it's about to remove?

contentSections.body: Before approving a plan, ask specifically: does anything after this destructive step still need what it's about to remove?

title: Steps that need a human between them
description: Recognizing which steps in a plan are mechanical enough for an agent to run straight through, and which ones need a person's judgment in the loop before the next step starts.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a mechanical step from a judgment step within a multi-step plan
Place human check-in points at judgment steps rather than uniformly or not at all

contentSections.title: Not every step is the same kind of step

contentSections.body: A six-step plan to add a new pricing tier. Steps 1, 2, 3, and 5 are: add a database column, add an API field, update the pricing calculation to branch on the new tier, update the tests. Step 4 is: "decide what happens to existing customers on the tier being split — grandfather them at the old price, migrate them automatically, or notify them and require action." An agent given the whole plan to run unattended will pick one of those three options and keep going, because a plan handed over as one instruction has no built-in place to stop and ask. It might pick the option a support team would have vetoed on sight. It will not flag that it picked anything at all — from its output, the step will read exactly like steps 1, 2, 3, and 5: done.

Most steps in a real plan are mechanical: given the inputs, there's one clearly correct way to do them, and an agent doing that work unattended carries little risk beyond ordinary implementation bugs, which the verification conditions from earlier lessons already catch. A smaller number of steps are judgment steps: the inputs alone don't determine a single correct answer, because the actual decision depends on something outside the code — a business tradeoff, a legal or compliance line, an irreversible choice about real users or real money, something only a person has the standing or the context to decide.

The mistake isn't running an agent unattended through a plan. It's failing to notice, while writing the plan, which of its steps are secretly judgment steps dressed up in the same flat, matter-of-fact language as the mechanical ones. "Handle existing customers on the old tier" reads exactly like "add a database column" in a numbered list. Only one of them has a single correct implementation waiting to be written; the other has three or four defensible answers and a real cost to picking wrong.

contentSections.scenario: A six-step plan for retiring an internal API that three other services still call.
contentSections.question: Select every step below that needs a human decision before the agent proceeds, rather than being safe to run straight through.

items.label: "Add a deprecation warning header to every response from the old API"
"Identify every caller of the old API across the codebase and list them"
"Decide which of the three calling services can migrate immediately versus which need a compatibility shim, based on how much each one's release schedule can absorb right now"
"Once every caller has migrated, delete the old API's code and its route registration"
"Write the migration guide describing the new API's request/response shape"

explanation.s1: Mechanical — adding a header is a single well-defined change with no branching decision behind it.
explanation.s2: Mechanical — a search-and-list task with an objectively checkable output (either the list is complete or it's missing something a code search would catch).
explanation.s3: This is a judgment step wearing a checklist's clothing. "How much each service's release schedule can absorb" is not information sitting in the codebase — it depends on other teams' plans, priorities, and constraints an agent has no visibility into and no standing to decide on their behalf.
explanation.s4: A destructive, hard-to-reverse step gating on a fact ("every caller has migrated") that's easy to get subtly wrong — a caller found through a code search might miss a caller only reachable through a config-driven route or an external partner integration. Even with a clean verification condition, this is exactly the kind of irreversible step from the previous lesson that benefits from a person confirming the precondition before it runs, not just an agent's own check of it.
explanation.s5: Mechanical — documenting a known, already-decided API shape is a writing task with a checkable output (does the guide match the actual request/response format), not a decision.

contentSections.body: A step written in the same flat language as the mechanical ones around it can still be a judgment step in disguise — check what the step actually depends on, not how it reads.

contentSections.title: Where to put the checkpoint

contentSections.body:
Once a plan's judgment steps are identified, the checkpoint goes immediately before each one, not at the end of the whole run. An agent that reaches a judgment step, makes a plausible-sounding choice, and then builds four more steps on top of that choice has already spent the cost of a wrong guess by the time a human looks at the final result — the same problem this whole module keeps returning to, just relocated to a single step instead of an entire task. The fix is the same fix: stop *before* the risky part, not after everything downstream of it has already been built.

In practice this means a plan's step list should mark, for each judgment step, what specific question needs a human answer and what information the agent should surface to make that answer possible — not just "stop and ask," but "stop, and here are the three migration-cost tradeoffs I found for each calling service, pick one." A checkpoint that hands the human a blank decision with no supporting information just moves the guessing from the agent to a person who now has to do the agent's research first.

contentSections.question: A plan's checkpoint just says: "Step 4 needs human input before proceeding." Nothing else. Before reading on: what's missing that would make this checkpoint actually useful to whoever has to answer it?
contentSections.answer: The specific question being asked, and the information needed to answer it — which calling services were found, what each one's migration cost looks like, what the tradeoffs are. Without that, the checkpoint just moves the agent's research burden onto the human instead of removing the risk.
contentSections.hint: Think about what you'd actually need in front of you to answer a judgment question in thirty seconds instead of having to go dig up the context yourself first.

contentSections.body: Put the checkpoint immediately before the judgment step, not at the end of the run — and hand the human the information needed to decide, not just the request to decide.

title: Writing the plan before anything runs
description: Turning everything from this module — small checkable steps, cheap-first ordering, marked judgment points — into one written artefact the agent works from and you approve before execution starts.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a written step-by-step plan with a verification condition, order rationale, and human check-in points marked, before any step executes

contentSections.title: The plan is a deliverable, not a formality

contentSections.body: Two ways to start the same piece of work. First: type the task into an agent and watch it go. Second: ask the agent to produce a written plan — the steps, in order, each with what "done" looks like — and read that plan before anything executes. The first approach costs nothing up front and a great deal after, if the plan the agent silently picked turns out to have the SDK call sites in the wrong order, or the destructive drop before the step that needed the data, or a judgment call buried where you'd never notice it until the diff was already forty files long. The second approach costs ten minutes of reading, at a point where every mistake in it is still just text — nothing has run yet, nothing has to be undone.

A written plan is where every skill from this module actually gets used, on paper, before it costs anything to have gotten one of them wrong: are the steps small enough to check individually (lesson 1)? Does each one have a real verification condition, not a restatement (lesson 2)? Is the order chosen so a wrong assumption surfaces before it's expensive, and are destructive steps pushed as late as the dependencies allow (lesson 3)? Are the judgment steps marked, with the checkpoint placed immediately before them and the supporting information the human will need already gathered (lesson 4)?

A plan that only lists step titles skips the part that actually catches problems — the verification conditions and the order rationale are what let a reader find the SDK-signature assumption or the backfill-after-drop mistake by reading, in under a minute, rather than by watching the run fail. The plan is worth writing out fully, as its own artefact, precisely because a bad plan is far cheaper to fix as a paragraph than as a completed run.

contentSections.problem: Write a plan for: "Add email verification to signup — new accounts should be unverified until they click a link, and unverified accounts can't post content."

steps.label: List the steps, ordered cheap/reversible-first
steps.work: 1. Add an `emailVerified: false` default to new user records (reversible, no behavior change yet). 2. Add a verification token generation + emailed link on signup (still no gating — testable in isolation by requesting an account and checking the email/token). 3. Add the verification endpoint that flips `emailVerified` to true on a valid token (testable against the token from step 2). 4. Gate content-posting on `emailVerified` (the only behavior-changing, could-lock-out-real-users step — placed last, after the first three are confirmed working).
steps.why: Steps 1–3 build and prove the verification mechanism works without changing what any existing feature does. Step 4 is the one step that could break something for real users if the mechanism underneath it is wrong, so it's held until that mechanism is proven.

steps.label: Attach a verification condition to each step
steps.work: Step 1: a newly created test user's record shows `emailVerified: false`. Step 2: signing up with a test address results in an email containing a token; the token exists in the database against that user. Step 3: hitting the verification endpoint with that exact token sets `emailVerified: true` for that user; hitting it with a fabricated token returns an error and changes nothing. Step 4: an unverified test user's POST to create content is rejected; the same user, after completing step 3's flow, can post successfully.
steps.why: Each condition names a specific action and a specific, checkable before/after — none of them are restatements of the step title.

steps.label: Mark the judgment step, if any
steps.work: One judgment question surfaces here: what happens to accounts that existed *before* this feature shipped — are they grandfathered as verified, or do they get locked out of posting until they verify retroactively? That's a product decision, not an implementation detail, so it's marked as a checkpoint before step 4 ships, with both options and their tradeoffs written out for whoever decides.
steps.why: This is exactly the kind of step that looks mechanical ("gate posting on verification") but is quietly a judgment step once existing accounts are considered — the plan surfaces it explicitly rather than letting step 4 decide it by default.

faded.problem: Write the plan, in the same shape, for: "Add a 'soft delete' to the comments feature — deleted comments should disappear from the UI but stay in the database for 30 days before permanent removal."

blanks.prompt: What's the reversible, low-risk step to do first?
blanks.answer: Add a `deletedAt` (nullable timestamp) column to comments, with nothing yet reading or writing it.
accept: add a nullable deletedAt column, no behavior change yet
blanks.why: Same pattern as lesson 3's shared-table example: the schema change alone, before anything depends on it, is the cheapest possible first move.

blanks.prompt: What's the step that should come last, and why?
blanks.answer: Permanently removing rows where `deletedAt` is more than 30 days old — this is the irreversible step, held until the soft-delete and UI-filtering steps are proven to correctly mark and hide comments first.
accept: the permanent-deletion job, run last because it's irreversible
blanks.why: Exactly the destructive-step-last rule from lesson 3 — nothing should permanently delete anything until the rest of the mechanism is confirmed to be marking the right rows.

blanks.prompt: Is there a judgment step here, and if so, what is it?
blanks.answer: Yes — what happens to a comment's replies when the parent is soft-deleted (also hide them, or leave them visible with a placeholder like "[deleted]")? That's a product/UX call, not something the code can derive on its own, and should be a marked checkpoint rather than an assumption baked silently into the UI-filtering step.
accept: how to handle replies to a deleted comment is a judgment call, not implementation detail
blanks.why: Same shape as the worked example's grandfathering question — a step that reads as pure implementation ("hide deleted comments") has a real decision hiding inside it once a realistic edge case (replies) is considered.

contentSections.procedure: Order steps cheap/reversible first, destructive last; attach a real verification condition to every step; scan the whole list for any step whose correct answer depends on something outside the code, and mark it as a checkpoint before it runs.

contentSections.body: A plan is worth writing as its own artefact because every mistake caught while reading it is a mistake that never had to be undone.

contentSections.title: What a written plan is not

contentSections.body:
A written plan is not a guarantee, and treating it as one defeats the point of the rest of this track — verifying each step's actual result still matters exactly as much as it would without a plan; a good plan makes verification easier to do, it doesn't replace it. Nor is a plan meant to anticipate every possible failure in advance; it's meant to name the steps, their check conditions, their order, and their judgment points clearly enough that when something *does* go wrong, it's visible at one specific step rather than smeared across an entire unbroken run.

A plan also isn't something to over-invest in for its own sake. A three-step task with no destructive step and no judgment call doesn't need the same ceremony as the twelve-call-site SDK migration — the amount of planning a task deserves scales with how expensive a wrong assumption in it would be to discover late, not with the raw size of the task. The skill this module is building is judgment about when and how much to plan, not a habit of writing plans regardless of whether the task calls for one.

contentSections.question: A task is: rename one internal helper function, used in exactly one file, no callers elsewhere. Before reading on: does this task need a written staged plan with marked judgment points, per this lesson's own rule?
contentSections.answer: No — it has no destructive or hard-to-reverse step and no judgment call, so a wrong assumption in it is cheap to spot and cheap to undo regardless. The planning ceremony this module teaches is worth its cost specifically when a task has multiple files, an irreversible step, or a real judgment call — not by default.
contentSections.hint: Go back to what actually determines how much planning a task deserves — it isn't the raw existence of the task, it's what a wrong assumption in it would cost to discover late.

contentSections.body: A plan earns its ten minutes by making mistakes visible while they're still just text — it doesn't replace checking the actual result of each step once it runs.

title: Decompose seven feature requests into verifiable steps
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given a feature request, either write or judge a decomposition against this module's four checks — small and checkable, real verification conditions, cheap/reversible-first order, and marked judgment points.

learningObjectives.text: Apply decomposition, verification-condition, ordering, and judgment-point identification skills at speed against unfamiliar feature requests

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills pulling on this module's four checks, in no particular order of difficulty — done in one sitting or spread out, nothing here expires.
If a drill needed the hint before the pattern clicked, that's the one worth watching for in your own next plan — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Plan a multi-file change as a step chain with checkpoints
description: Take a real multi-file change you actually need, and write the full plan for it — ordered steps, a verification condition for each, and every judgment point marked — before running any of it through an agent.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a complete, ordered step plan for a genuine multi-file change, with a verification condition attached to every step
Identify and mark every judgment point in a real plan, with the supporting information a human would need to decide

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every example this module used was already decomposed for you. This lab closes that gap: pick a real change you actually need — spanning at least three files or components — and write its full plan yourself, from a blank page, before anything runs.

contentSections.title: Plan a multi-file change as a step chain with checkpoints
contentSections.brief: Pick a real change you genuinely want made to something you're working on — it should touch at least three files or components and have at least one step that's either destructive/hard-to-reverse or a genuine judgment call, not just implementation. Examples if you need one: adding a new required field to a shared data model consumed by multiple parts of a system, retiring an old code path in favor of a new one, or adding a permission check that changes existing behavior for some users. Write the complete step chain before running any of it.
contentSections.deliverable: A written plan: an ordered list of steps, each with a concrete verification condition (an input, an expected observable output, not a restatement of the step). At least one destructive or hard-to-reverse step, positioned as late as its real dependencies allow. Every judgment point explicitly marked, with the specific question and the information a human would need to decide it written out alongside.

stages.title: Scope the change and list the raw steps
stages.instructions: Write down the change in one or two sentences, then list every step you can think of that it requires, in any order for now. Don't filter or refine yet — get the full raw list down first.
stages.checkpoint: A raw list of steps exists, covering the change end to end, even if the order and granularity aren't right yet.

stages.title: Size and order the steps
stages.instructions: Break any step that isn't independently checkable into smaller pieces (lesson 1). Reorder the list so cheap, assumption-revealing work comes first and any destructive or hard-to-reverse step comes as late as its real dependencies allow (lesson 3). Check explicitly: does anything later in the plan depend on something an earlier destructive step removes?
stages.checkpoint: Every step in the list is small enough to check on its own, and the order has been deliberately checked against the cheap-first, destructive-last rule — not just left in whatever order it was first written.

stages.title: Attach verification conditions
stages.instructions: For every step, write "this step is done when ___" with a specific input and observable output — not a restatement of the step title. Aim each one at the part of the step most likely to be silently wrong (lesson 2), not just at whether the step ran.
stages.checkpoint: Every step has a verification condition that names a concrete input and output, and at least one of them is aimed at a specific numeric threshold, edge case, or rule rather than just "the feature works."

stages.title: Mark judgment points and self-check
stages.instructions: Reread the whole plan looking specifically for any step whose correct answer depends on something outside the code — a tradeoff, a policy, an irreversible choice about real data or real users. Mark each one as a checkpoint, with the specific question and the information needed to answer it. Self-check the whole plan against the rubric below.
stages.checkpoint: Every judgment point in the plan is explicitly marked, not left implicit inside a step that reads as purely mechanical.

rubric.criterion: Every step is independently checkable
rubric.meets: A reader could look at any single step's verification condition and know whether that step succeeded, without needing to read the rest of the plan or the eventual diff.

rubric.criterion: Every verification condition is specific, not a restatement
rubric.meets: Each one names a concrete input and a concrete observable output — not just a repetition of the step's title in slightly different words.

rubric.criterion: The order is deliberately cheap/reversible-first, destructive-last
rubric.meets: The plan can state, for its one destructive or hard-to-reverse step, exactly what earlier steps needed to be confirmed first and why nothing later still depends on what that step removes.

rubric.criterion: At least one genuine judgment point is identified and marked
rubric.meets: A step whose correct answer isn't determined by the code alone is called out explicitly, with the specific question and the information a human would need to answer it — not folded silently into a step that looks mechanical.

rubric.criterion: The plan is usable as an actual instruction set, not just a description of the change
rubric.meets: Someone other than you could hand this plan to an agent step by step and know, after each one, whether to proceed — without needing the original change request in front of them.

contentSections.body: A plan that survives its own self-check against this rubric is a plan you can hand to an agent one step at a time with a real answer, at every step, for 'how do I know this worked.'

title: Checkpoint — Decomposition and Task Design
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Error Handling and Failure Paths (the module immediately before this one), two from The Bugs AI Writes Most, further back in the track.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's decomposition, verification-condition, and ordering patterns alongside earlier modules' failure-handling and defect patterns, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Decomposition and Task Design

questions.from: This module — Decomposition and Task Design
questions.prompt: Two plans touch the same twelve files. Plan A tests the riskiest assumption on file one before touching the other eleven; Plan B touches all twelve then tests everything at once. Why is Plan A less risky, given they change the same code overall?

options.label: Because a wrong assumption in Plan A is discovered and fixed before it's copied into eleven more places, where in Plan B it's already everywhere by the time anyone checks
It isn't actually less risky — total scope of change is what determines risk, not order
Because Plan A takes less total time to execute

questions.explanation: Order changes where in the sequence a wrong assumption becomes visible, and how much has been built on top of it by then — not the total amount of work. The same defect costs one fix in Plan A and twelve in Plan B.

questions.from: This module — Decomposition and Task Design
questions.prompt: A step's verification condition reads: "done when the export feature works." What's wrong with it?

options.label: It restates the step rather than naming a specific, checkable input and output
Nothing — a condition just needs to confirm the feature exists
It's too long and should be shortened

questions.explanation: "Works" names no observable fact to check against. A real condition names a concrete input (a known fixture) and a concrete, comparable output — something you could check without trusting a summary.

questions.from: This module — Decomposition and Task Design
questions.prompt: A plan step reads: "decide whether to grandfather existing customers at the old price or migrate them automatically." Why does this step need a human checkpoint, even though it's written in the same flat style as the mechanical steps around it?

options.label: Its correct answer depends on a business tradeoff outside the code, not something derivable from the codebase alone
It doesn't — any step that can be phrased as an instruction is safe for an agent to run unattended
Because it involves customers, and any customer-facing step always needs approval

questions.explanation: The test for a judgment step isn't its wording or its subject matter — it's whether the inputs alone determine one correct answer. A pricing/migration tradeoff depends on information (support capacity, business priorities) an agent has no access to and no standing to decide.

questions.from: This module — Decomposition and Task Design
questions.prompt: Why does a destructive step (like dropping an old database table) generally belong last in a plan rather than wherever it fits most naturally by task logic?

options.label: Because it's hard or impossible to reverse, so every step that might reveal a wrong assumption should run first, while reversing is still cheap
Destructive steps should be run first to get the risky part out of the way early
Order doesn't actually matter as long as every step eventually runs

questions.explanation: Reversible steps first, destructive last: every step that could surface "this whole approach was wrong" gets the chance to do so while undoing it still just means not running the next step, rather than recovering from data that's already gone.

questions.from: Previous module — Error Handling and Failure Paths
questions.prompt: A generated catch block does `catch (err) { return null; }` and the caller checks `if (result) { ... }`. What does this pattern actually hide?

options.label: Every distinct failure — a timeout, a 404, a malformed response — collapses into the same signal as a legitimate empty result, so the caller can't tell 'nothing found' from 'something broke'
Nothing — returning null on error is a safe, conventional pattern in most languages
Only network errors are actually swallowed by this pattern; other error types still propagate

questions.explanation: Swallowing every error into the same falsy return erases the distinction between an empty-but-successful result and a failure — the caller has no way to recover appropriately, retry, or surface the real problem, because the specific error was thrown away at the exact point it was known.

questions.from: Previous module — Error Handling and Failure Paths
questions.prompt: A multi-step signup writes a user row, then a workspace row, then calls a billing API — and the billing call fails. What does 'partial failure' mean here?

options.label: The user and workspace rows already committed and now exist with no corresponding billing record, unless something explicitly detects and repairs that state
The entire operation automatically rolls back across all three steps, including the external billing call
Partial failure only matters if the billing API returns a 500 rather than timing out

questions.explanation: A database transaction, if one is even in play, only covers database operations — it has no power to undo an external API call. Without an explicit compensation or detection step, a failure partway through a multi-step write leaves the earlier, already-committed steps in place with nothing to reconcile them.

questions.from: Previous module — Error Handling and Failure Paths
questions.prompt: Why does a good error message for an on-call engineer look different from a good error message for an end user?

options.label: The engineer needs enough specific, technical detail to locate the failure at 3am with no other context; the user needs to know what to do next, not the internals
There's no real difference — one well-written error message serves both audiences equally well
User-facing messages should always include the full stack trace so support can escalate faster

questions.explanation: These are different audiences with different needs at different moments — an engineer paged at 3am needs the specific failing call, the input that triggered it, and enough context to reproduce it; a user needs a plain statement of what happened and what to do, not internals that mean nothing to them and may leak information besides.

questions.from: Previous module — Error Handling and Failure Paths
questions.prompt: A generated retry loop retries a failed request immediately, three times, with no delay between attempts. What's the risk specific to this pattern under a real outage?

options.label: A struggling service gets hit with a burst of immediate retries from every failing caller at once, which can turn a partial outage into a complete one
There's no real risk — retrying more times only ever increases the odds of eventual success
The risk only applies to database calls, not HTTP requests

questions.explanation: Immediate, undelayed retries synchronize load exactly when a service is least able to handle it — this is what backoff (increasing delay between attempts) and jitter (randomizing it slightly) exist to prevent, by spreading retries out instead of amplifying the exact moment of failure.

questions.from: Three modules back — The Bugs AI Writes Most
questions.prompt: A generated retry helper is `for attempt in range(max_retries):` with `max_retries = 3`. How many total attempts does this actually make?

options.label: 3 — range(3) yields exactly three values, so the loop body runs three times total, regardless of what the variable name implies
4 — the name 'max_retries' implies retries in addition to the first attempt
It depends on whether the first attempt is counted separately elsewhere in the code

questions.explanation: `range(3)` yields 0, 1, 2 — three iterations. The variable name suggests a convention the code doesn't actually implement; counting what the loop does, not what the name implies, is the only reliable check.

questions.from: Three modules back — The Bugs AI Writes Most
questions.prompt: A generated checkout function has zero conditionals and operates on a list of cart items. What should that absence of branching make you check first?

options.label: What happens when the list is empty — the single most common non-happy-path state a function meets
Whether the function's variable names are descriptive enough
Whether the function is fast enough for a large cart

questions.explanation: Zero conditionals in an edge-case-heavy domain is the structural tell for happy-path-only code, and an empty collection is usually the single most common non-happy-path input a function actually meets in production.

title: What the agent can reach is what it can break
description: Blast radius is set by what an agent is granted access to, not by what the task description says it's supposed to do — and those two things quietly diverge more often than they match.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an agent's blast radius is defined by its granted access, not by its assigned task
Identify the gap between a task's intended scope and the scope its actual permissions allow

contentSections.title: "Clean up temp files" reaches further than temp files

contentSections.body: You ask an agent, with full filesystem access to your home directory, to "clean up temp files in the project." It runs `find . -name "*.tmp" -o -name "*.cache" -delete` from what it believes is the project root — except the shell session's working directory had drifted one command earlier to your home directory itself, and `.cache` happens to also match a directory your terminal multiplexer, your language server, and two other tools store real state in. The task was four words. The access was your entire home directory. The damage was set by the second thing, not the first.

An agent's blast radius — the full set of things a mistake could actually touch — is determined by what it's been granted access to, not by what its current task is trying to do. A task description is a statement of intent; a permission grant is a statement of possibility. These are frequently treated as if they were the same thing, because most of the time an agent's actions do stay inside the intended scope — right up until a wrong assumption, a working-directory mixup, or an overly broad glob pattern uses the *possible* instead of the *intended*.

This is not a claim that agents are unusually careless. A human running the same command from the same broadened access would make the identical mistake under the identical conditions — a slipped working directory plus a pattern that's broader than it looks is a classic shell error regardless of who or what is typing it. What's different with an agent is the volume and speed: a human typically issues one risky command and looks at the result before the next one; an agent given a multi-step task can issue a chain of them, unattended, before anyone looks at any of it.

contentSections.scenario: An agent is given read/write access to `~/projects/` (not scoped to a single project) and asked to "add a .gitignore entry for build artifacts in the reports-app project." It runs a script that walks the given path looking for a `.git` directory to confirm it's in a repo, doesn't find one at the exact level it expected, walks up one more directory, finds `~/projects/.git` instead — a monorepo wrapper you'd forgotten was there — and commits its .gitignore change there, silently affecting every project underneath it.
contentSections.question: What's the actual root cause here?

options.label: The agent was granted access to the whole `~/projects/` tree when the task only needed one project inside it
The script's directory-walking logic is buggy and should be fixed before this happens again
The task description should have said 'only the reports-app project' more explicitly

feedback.over-broad-access: Right. Fixing the script's walk-up behavior or wording the task more precisely both reduce the *chance* of this specific mistake, but neither changes what's actually reachable if something else goes wrong next time. Scoping access to exactly the reports-app directory means a wrong assumption in the walk-up logic has nowhere else to land — the monorepo `.git` simply isn't inside what the agent can touch.
feedback.bad-script: A real bug, and worth fixing — but fixing this one walk-up quirk doesn't address the underlying condition that made it dangerous: an agent operating with access far broader than the task needed. The next bug, in a different tool, would find the same broad access waiting.
feedback.bad-task-wording: More precise wording lowers the odds the agent chooses to act outside the intended scope — it does nothing about whether it's *able* to. Task wording is about intent; only the granted access controls what's actually possible when intent and execution diverge.

contentSections.mechanism: A permission grant should be sized to the task, not to convenience — because the cost of a mistake is set by the boundary of what's reachable, not by how carefully the instruction was worded. The reports-app task never needed anything above the reports-app directory; giving it anyway created a blast radius the task itself had no use for.

contentSections.body: The size of a possible mistake is set by what's reachable, not by what the task says it intends to do — scope access to the task, not to convenience.

contentSections.title: Convenience is the reason scope creeps

contentSections.body:
Granting broad access up front is nearly always the path of least resistance in the moment — it avoids the friction of hitting a permission wall mid-task and having to stop and widen it. That friction is not a flaw to route around; it's the one moment where a person notices the agent needs something beyond what was originally scoped, and can decide, specifically, whether that's actually warranted. Removing the friction by granting broad access up front removes the checkpoint along with it.

The practical habit: start every agent task with the narrowest access that could plausibly complete it, and treat a permission error mid-run as useful information — either the task genuinely needs more than expected (and now you know exactly what, and can grant exactly that), or the agent has wandered outside the intended scope (and you've just caught it before it went further).

contentSections.question: An agent hits a permission error mid-task: it tried to write to a path outside its granted scope. Before reading on: what are the two genuinely different explanations for why that happened, and how would you tell which one it is?
contentSections.answer: Either the task legitimately needs that extra access (check what it was trying to write and why, then grant exactly that) or the agent has drifted outside the intended scope (in which case the error just caught a mistake before it went further). Reading what it was actually trying to do at that path is what tells you which.
contentSections.hint: One explanation means widen the grant; the other means something already went wrong and the wall just caught it in time.

contentSections.body: A permission error mid-task is useful information, not friction to eliminate — it tells you either what to widen, precisely, or that something drifted outside scope.

title: Read, write, execute, network: granting the minimum
description: Four separate dimensions of access — reading, writing, executing, and reaching the network — and why granting all four by default is rarely what any given task actually needs.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish read, write, execute, and network access as four separate grants, each scoped independently
Scope an agent's access to the minimum combination of the four a specific task requires

contentSections.title: Four different questions, one default answer

contentSections.body: "Give the agent access to the repo" sounds like one decision. It's actually at least four: can it read files (see what's there), can it write files (change what's there), can it execute commands (run scripts, install packages, invoke a shell), and can it reach the network (call an API, download a package, push to a remote). A code-review task needs exactly one of those four — read. Granting all four because that's what "access to the repo" defaults to in most setups means a review task, which never needed to write, run, or reach anywhere, is now one wrong tool call away from doing any of the three.

Treating these as four independent dimensions, each granted only where the task actually needs it, is the core move of this lesson. Read access lets an agent see file contents and answer questions about them — safe on its own, since nothing about reading changes state. Write access lets it modify files — necessary for any task that produces a diff, and the first dimension where a mistake has a lasting effect. Execute access lets it run commands: tests, scripts, package installs, arbitrary shell — this is where a mistake can affect things well outside the files it can see, because a shell command's effects aren't bounded by a file-access scope at all. Network access lets it reach anything outside the local environment — pull a dependency, call an external API, exfiltrate something, depending entirely on what's on the other end.

A task's actual dimension needs are usually a small subset of all four. Reviewing code: read only. Fixing a typo in one file: read and write, no execute, no network. Running a test suite to check a fix: read, write, execute, still no network unless the tests themselves call out. Installing a new dependency: all four, because a package install both executes and reaches the network. The habit is naming, for each task, which of the four it genuinely needs — not defaulting to whatever the tool's broadest preset happens to bundle together.

contentSections.intro: Task: "Check whether the changes on this feature branch pass the existing test suite, and report which tests fail." Build the minimal permission grant, one dimension at a time.

fields.prompt: Does this task need read access?

options.label: Yes
No

feedback.yes: Right — it has to see the code and the test files to run anything against them.
feedback.no: It can't run a test suite it can't see. Read access is required here.

fields.prompt: Does this task need write access?

options.label: Yes
No

feedback.no: Right — running an existing test suite and reporting failures never requires modifying any file. If the agent wants to write anything, that's outside this task's actual scope.
feedback.yes: Nothing about running and reporting on an existing suite requires modifying a file. Granting write here is broader than the task, not because of anything the task needs.

fields.prompt: Does this task need execute access?

options.label: Yes
No

feedback.yes: Right — running a test suite is, definitionally, executing something. This is the one dimension the task can't be done without.
feedback.no: Running the test suite is exactly what execute access is for; there's no way to do this task without it.

fields.prompt: Does this task need network access?

options.label: Yes
No

feedback.no: Right, assuming dependencies are already installed — running an existing suite against existing code touches nothing outside the local environment.
feedback.yes: Only if dependencies still need installing first, which isn't what this task described. As stated — run the existing suite — nothing here reaches outside the local machine.

contentSections.synthesis: Read + execute, no write, no network. Naming all four explicitly, even the two the task doesn't need, is what makes the "no" answers deliberate decisions rather than defaults nobody looked at.

contentSections.body: Name all four dimensions for every task, even the ones the answer is 'no' — a deliberate 'no' is a decision; a default 'yes' nobody looked at is scope creep.

contentSections.title: The dimension that travels furthest

contentSections.body:
Execute and network deserve extra scrutiny beyond read and write, because their effects aren't bounded by the files an agent can see. Write access, however broad, is still bounded by the filesystem paths it covers — a mistake there is bad, but it's contained to what's readable and writable in that scope. Execute access lets an agent run *anything* the underlying shell can run, which on most systems is not bounded by the project directory at all — a script can read environment variables holding credentials for services that have nothing to do with the current task, or invoke a system command that affects the whole machine. Network access compounds this further: once a process can reach outward, whatever it can read locally (including anything execute access exposed) can, in principle, leave the machine entirely.

The practical implication: read and write scope to a *path*. Execute and network scope to a *capability* that isn't naturally bounded by a path at all, and usually need a different mechanism — a restricted shell, an explicit command allowlist, a network policy — to actually contain them, rather than trusting that "it only has access to this folder" also constrains what a command run from that folder can reach.

contentSections.question: The filesystem grant is correctly scoped to read-only. What's still wrong with this config for a read-only review task?

options.label: "shell: unrestricted" grants execute access with no scoping at all, which isn't bounded by the read-only filesystem path and can reach far beyond it
The filesystem path is scoped too narrowly and should include more of the workspace
Nothing — the read-only filesystem restriction already covers what a review task needs

feedback.unrestricted-shell: Correct. A review task needs zero shell commands to read files and report on them. "Unrestricted" shell access means any command the underlying system allows can run — including ones that read environment variables, reach the network, or write to paths entirely outside `/workspace/reports-app`. The read-only filesystem grant is doing nothing to contain what an unrestricted shell can do.
feedback.path-too-narrow: The path is exactly right for a review task scoped to reports-app — the problem isn't that the filesystem grant is too narrow, it's that the shell grant next to it isn't scoped at all, and shell access isn't bounded by that filesystem path.
feedback.fine-as-is: The filesystem line is fine; the shell line undoes most of its value. A read-only file grant provides no protection against a command that never touches the filesystem at all — reading a credential from an environment variable, or making an outbound network call, for instance.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This config makes the common mistake of treating "scope the filesystem" as if it scopes everything. The fix names the shell dimension explicitly, the same way the filesystem dimension was named: `"shell": {"mode": "disabled"}` for a task that genuinely needs zero commands, or an explicit allowlist of specific, harmless commands (e.g. a linter, a formatter check) if some execution really is required — never "unrestricted" as a default sitting next to a carefully scoped filesystem line.

contentSections.body: Read and write scope to a path; execute and network scope to a capability that isn't naturally bounded by one — each needs its own explicit restriction, not just an assumption that the filesystem grant covers it.

title: Working on a branch, a copy, or a container
description: Three levels of isolation for agent work, and matching the level to how much a task's mistakes should be able to reach — from a git branch protecting tracked code, up to a container isolating the whole environment.

learningObjectives.text: Match an isolation level (branch, copy, container) to a task's actual blast radius

contentSections.title: Three different things "isolated" can mean

contentSections.body: "Run it in isolation" gets used for three genuinely different setups. A git branch isolates tracked code changes from `main` — cheap, instant, and reversible with `git checkout main`, but it does nothing about files outside version control, installed packages, or anything the agent's shell commands touch beyond the repo. A copy of a working directory isolates the whole directory, tracked or not — safer for tasks that touch build artifacts, local config, or generated files a branch wouldn't cover, but still shares the host machine's installed tools, network access, and everything else outside that one directory. A container isolates the entire runtime environment — filesystem, process space, and (if configured) network — so a mistake inside it can't reach the host machine at all, at real setup cost.

None of the three is universally correct; each is proportionate to a different blast radius. A task that only ever edits tracked source files and runs no shell commands beyond the project's own test runner is well served by a branch — cheap, and the one thing that could really go wrong (bad code) is exactly what the branch boundary protects against. A task that also touches `.env` files, writes to a local cache, or generates artifacts outside git needs at least a full directory copy, because a branch's protection stops at what git tracks. A task that installs new packages, runs arbitrary shell commands, or reaches the network for anything beyond a known dependency install is the one that benefits from a container — because at that point the actual risk isn't confined to files at all.

Choosing too little isolation for a task's real risk is the obvious mistake — running an agent that installs packages and runs shell scripts directly against your primary working directory with no container. The less obvious mistake is choosing too much: wrapping a two-line text-edit task in full container setup costs real time and adds a layer to work around later, for a task whose entire actual risk a branch already fully covers.
Match isolation to blast radius — under-isolating a shell-and-network task is dangerous, but over-isolating a two-line edit is its own real cost.

contentSections.title: A branch is not a sandbox

contentSections.body: The most common mistake here isn't picking the wrong level — it's assuming a git branch provides more protection than it actually does. A branch protects `main` from bad commits. It provides zero protection against a shell command the agent runs while working on that branch: `rm -rf node_modules`, a script that writes to `/tmp` or beyond, a package install that runs an arbitrary post-install script — none of that is undone by `git checkout main`, because none of it was ever tracked by git in the first place. "It's on a branch" is sometimes treated as a green light for letting an agent run unrestricted shell commands, on the reasoning that anything it does is reversible — which is true for the commits, and false for everything else the shell touched along the way.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what's the one question worth checking before trusting a git branch as sufficient isolation for a given task?
contentSections.answer: Does this task's plan include any step with execute or network access? If yes, a branch alone doesn't match that task's real blast radius — a branch and a container are answering two different questions, and only a purely code-editing task actually needs just the first.
contentSections.hint: A branch only ever protects one specific thing — think about what that is, and what a task's other steps might do that a branch has no power over.

contentSections.body: A branch protects commits, not the shell — check whether a task's steps ever grant execute or network access before trusting a branch as isolation enough.

title: Destructive operations that need a human hand on them
description: A specific category of operation — the ones that destroy data, revoke access, or move real money — that stay behind a human confirmation regardless of how routine the surrounding task is.

learningObjectives.text: Identify operations whose worst case is irreversible enough that they should never run without an explicit human confirmation
Distinguish a destructive operation gated by a human check from one merely logged after the fact

contentSections.title: Some operations don't get to be routine

contentSections.body: An agent handling routine cleanup finds a database table it believes is unused — no recent writes, no obvious application code referencing it — and, as part of a broader "clean up dead schema objects" task, drops it. The table was a nightly export destination for a reporting pipeline that reads it, not writes to it, so "no recent writes" looked exactly like "unused" from the angle the agent checked. The table is gone. The pipeline that depended on it finds out the next morning.

Some categories of operation carry a worst case severe enough — genuinely irreversible, or reversible only at real cost — that they belong behind a human confirmation regardless of how confident the agent's reasoning looks, and regardless of how routine the surrounding task feels. Dropping a table or deleting a bucket. Force-pushing over history other people's work depends on. Rotating or revoking a credential other running services still hold a copy of. Deleting a cloud resource with data on it. Sending an irreversible external action — an email to a real customer list, a payment, a production deploy with no rollback path prepared.

What these share isn't complexity — dropping a table is a one-line command. What they share is that the cost of being wrong is not "redo it," the way a bad code change is; it's "recover from it," which for many of these is expensive, sometimes impossible, and if the previous lesson's isolation choice was matched to a lower risk than the task actually carried, it may not be contained to a sandbox at all.
