A gate on these operations isn't distrust of the agent's specific reasoning in this instance — the reasoning above (no recent writes therefore unused) is exactly the kind of reasoning a careful human reviewer might also produce, and might also get wrong for the same reason. It's a recognition that some mistakes are too expensive to let ride on any single check, human or automated, being right.

contentSections.scenario: A task plan for decommissioning an old service includes six operations.
contentSections.question: Select every operation below that belongs behind an explicit human confirmation before it runs, regardless of how confident the surrounding reasoning is.

items.label: Removing the old service's route from the API gateway config
Deleting the old service's production database, after confirming (via query) that it has had no writes in 90 days
Archiving the old service's source repository (read-only, fully recoverable by unarchiving)
Revoking the old service's API credentials with the upstream payment provider
Updating internal documentation to note the service is decommissioned
Force-pushing a cleaned-up commit history to the old service's now-archived repo, overwriting its existing history

explanation.s1: A config change, reversible by re-adding the route — the same low-stakes category as most of this module's other examples.
explanation.s2: "No writes in 90 days" is evidence, not proof of "safe to delete" — the reporting-pipeline example in this lesson's hook shows exactly how that inference can be wrong, and a deleted production database is not something "redo it" fixes.
explanation.s3: Archiving is explicitly reversible (unarchive), which is the whole reason it doesn't need the same gate as an operation whose reversal isn't built in.
explanation.s4: Revoking credentials another system might still be depending on, even one believed decommissioned, risks an outage somewhere unexpected if that belief is wrong — and revoked credentials aren't something you can quietly un-revoke back to the exact prior state.
explanation.s5: A documentation edit — reversible by editing it again, and carries no operational risk at all.
explanation.s6: Rewriting history is destructive to anything that still references the old commits (a fork, a pinned dependency, an old deploy tag) — "archived" doesn't mean "nothing else could still reference this," and a force-push here is not undoable once it's happened.

contentSections.body: The gate belongs on the category of operation — irreversible, or expensive to reverse — not on how confident the specific reasoning behind it happens to sound.

contentSections.title: A confirmation prompt is not a real gate

contentSections.body:
A human confirmation step only works as a real gate if the human answering it has enough information to actually evaluate the decision — not just enough to click through it. "About to drop table `legacy_exports` — confirm?" gives a person nothing to evaluate beyond the agent's own claim that it's fine; a rushed or distracted "yes" to that prompt provides no more real protection than no gate at all, and can be worse, because it creates the appearance of oversight without the substance of it.

A gate that actually functions surfaces the evidence behind the decision, not just the decision: "about to drop `legacy_exports` — no direct application writes found in 90 days; note this check does not cover read-only consumers like scheduled export jobs — confirm?" This is the same principle as the human checkpoints from the previous module's decomposition lessons, applied specifically to destructive operations: the checkpoint's value comes entirely from what it hands the person deciding, not from the mere fact that a prompt appeared.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what's the actual difference between a confirmation prompt that functions as a real gate and one that's just a rubber stamp?
contentSections.answer: A real gate surfaces the evidence behind the decision — what was checked, and what that check doesn't cover. A rubber stamp just states the pending action and asks yes/no, giving the person nothing to actually evaluate beyond the agent's own claim that it's fine.
contentSections.hint: Think about what you'd actually need in front of you to say more than a reflexive 'yes' to a deletion prompt.

contentSections.body: A confirmation prompt with no evidence behind it produces a rubber stamp, not a check — the gate's value is in what it tells the person deciding, not in the pause itself.

title: Recovering from an agent that did the wrong thing thoroughly
description: Establishing a real recovery path — reflog, backups, versioned state — before granting risky access, so the worst case is a bad afternoon instead of unrecoverable loss.

learningObjectives.text: Establish a concrete recovery mechanism appropriate to a task's blast radius before granting the access that makes it risky

contentSections.title: The recovery plan comes before the access, not after the damage

contentSections.body: An agent, mid-refactor, runs a cleanup script that deletes what it believes are unused local branches — and deletes one that had an afternoon of uncommitted-but-stashed work nobody had pushed anywhere. `git branch -D` doesn't ask twice. The commits themselves aren't necessarily gone — git's reflog holds recently deleted commit references for a window before garbage collection — but only if you know to look there, and only if nothing else has run `git gc` in the meantime. The difference between a bad ten minutes and a genuinely lost afternoon of work came down to whether a recovery path existed and was known about *before* the deletion happened, not to anything done after.

A recovery path decided after something has already gone wrong is being invented under pressure, often too late to matter — by the time you're searching for how to undo a dropped table, the honest answer may be "you can't, unless a backup exists and someone already knew where it was." The lesson from every prior one in this module converges here: scoping access, choosing isolation, and gating destructive operations all reduce how often something goes wrong and how far it can reach — none of them make the worst case impossible, and a genuine recovery plan is what determines whether the worst case, when it does happen, is recoverable at all.

Establishing recovery before granting access means answering, concretely, for the specific task about to run: if the worst plausible mistake happened right now, what's the actual, tested mechanism to undo it, and does it exist *before* the task starts — not "there's probably a backup somewhere." For code, that's usually git's own history plus the reflog window, so long as nothing's been force-cleaned in between. For a database, that's a snapshot or point-in-time recovery, confirmed to actually restore, not just configured to exist. For anything outside version control or a database's own backup mechanism, it might be a directory copy taken deliberately before the risky step runs — the same directory-copy isolation from lesson 3, now serving double duty as a restore point.

contentSections.problem: A task will let an agent run schema-changing migrations against a staging database with real, hard-to-regenerate seed data. Establish the recovery path before granting access.

steps.label: Name the worst plausible mistake for this specific task
steps.work: A migration that drops or truncates a table containing seed data that took real time to assemble and isn't trivially regeneratable from a script.
steps.why: The recovery plan has to be built for the actual worst case this task could produce, not a generic 'something goes wrong' — a migration task's worst case is specifically data loss from schema changes, not, say, a leaked credential.

steps.label: Identify the concrete, existing recovery mechanism for that specific worst case
steps.work: Confirm the database supports point-in-time recovery or has an automated daily snapshot — not "probably does," but checked, right now, that a specific recent snapshot exists and is restorable.
steps.why: A backup that's configured but never verified to actually restore is not a recovery mechanism, it's an assumption wearing a recovery mechanism's clothes — the only way to know it works is to have actually tried a restore against it.

steps.label: Take an extra, task-specific snapshot immediately before the risky step, don't rely solely on the general schedule
steps.work: Trigger a manual snapshot right before the migration runs, so the restore point is minutes old rather than however far back the last scheduled snapshot happened to fall.
steps.why: A daily snapshot from 20 hours ago might be missing a day's worth of legitimate changes that would also be lost on restore — a fresh, task-specific snapshot minimizes what a recovery would actually cost to redo.

faded.problem: A task will let an agent run a script that bulk-renames files across a shared network drive used by several people, not backed by git. Establish the recovery path.

blanks.prompt: Name the worst plausible mistake for this specific task.
blanks.answer: The rename script misidentifies which files match its pattern and renames (or overwrites) files other people are actively using, with no version history to fall back on.
accept: files get incorrectly renamed or overwritten with no git history to recover from
blanks.why: A shared, non-git-tracked drive has none of the git-based recovery this module leans on elsewhere — that absence is itself the key fact driving what recovery mechanism is needed.

blanks.prompt: What's the concrete recovery mechanism, given there's no git history here?
blanks.answer: A full copy of the affected directory taken immediately before the script runs, stored somewhere the rename script itself can't reach or affect.
accept: a pre-run directory copy stored outside the script's own reach
blanks.why: With no version control as a safety net, the directory-copy technique from lesson 3 becomes the actual recovery mechanism, not just an isolation choice — and it has to sit outside what the script itself can touch, or a bug in the script could damage the copy too.

blanks.prompt: What makes this recovery mechanism trustworthy rather than just assumed?
blanks.answer: Actually testing that a file can be restored from the copy before the real run starts — confirming the copy is complete and readable, not just that the copy command exited without an error.
accept: verifying the copy actually restores something before trusting it
blanks.why: Same principle as the database snapshot example — a copy or backup that's never been checked to actually work is an assumption, not a mechanism.

contentSections.procedure: For any risky task: name the worst plausible mistake specifically, confirm (not assume) a recovery mechanism already exists and actually works for that exact mistake, and take a fresh, task-specific safety point immediately before the risky step runs.

contentSections.body: A recovery plan invented after the damage is a plan invented under pressure, often too late — confirm the mechanism exists and actually works before the risky step runs, not after.

contentSections.title: "We have backups" is not the same claim as "we have a tested restore"

contentSections.body:
The gap between these two claims is where most recovery plans quietly fail. A backup job that has run successfully every night for a year proves the backup process itself doesn't error out — it proves nothing about whether the resulting backup can actually be restored into a working state, whether it captures everything that matters, or how long a real restore would take under pressure. An untested backup is scheduled optimism, not a recovery mechanism, and the only way to close that gap is to have actually restored from it at least once, deliberately, before trusting it as the safety net behind a risky agent task.

This closes the loop back to where the module started: blast radius is set by what's reachable, isolation and permission scoping reduce how much is reachable, destructive-operation gates catch the worst individual moves before they run — and a tested recovery path is what determines whether the whole system survives the case where all of that still wasn't enough. None of these substitute for each other; a task's actual safety is the combination.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: a team says "we have nightly backups" as their entire recovery plan. What specific gap makes that an incomplete answer?
contentSections.answer: A backup that has never actually been restored from proves the backup job runs without erroring — it proves nothing about whether the result actually restores into a working state. Only a deliberate, tested restore closes that gap.
contentSections.hint: Separate 'the backup process succeeded' from 'the backup actually works when you need it.'

contentSections.body: A backup that's never been restored from is an assumption, not a recovery mechanism — the only way to know it works is to have already tried it.

title: Set the permission boundary for eight agent tasks
description: Eight drills, no new concepts: given a task, choose the correct minimal permission and isolation setup against plausible over- or under-scoped alternatives.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the read/write/execute/network and isolation-level scoping rules from this module at speed against unfamiliar tasks

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills against this module's scoping rules, in no particular order of difficulty — done in one sitting or spread out, nothing here expires.
If a drill needed the hint before the scoping call was obvious, that's the pattern worth watching for the next time you set up a real agent task.

title: Configure a sandboxed workspace for an autonomous change
description: Build a real, working sandbox configuration for a genuine agent task, scoped to the minimum access it needs, plus a written recovery plan for its worst plausible failure.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a working sandbox configuration scoped to a real task's minimum read/write/execute/network needs
Write a concrete, verified recovery plan for a task's worst plausible failure before granting the access that makes it possible

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every scenario this module used was already scoped for you. This lab closes that gap: pick a real, somewhat risky autonomous task you'd actually want to hand an agent — one that involves at least an execute step, ideally something touching a real file tree or a real (non-production) database — and build its actual sandbox config and recovery plan from scratch.

contentSections.title: Configure a sandboxed workspace for an autonomous change
contentSections.brief: Pick a real task you'd genuinely want an agent to run with some autonomy — something with at least one execute step (running a script, installing something, running a build), touching either a real file tree or a non-production database/data store. Do not use production data or a task with real destructive stakes for this exercise; the point is to build the muscle, not to run the actual risky version. Build the sandbox configuration for it, and write out what recovery would look like if the worst plausible thing happened.
contentSections.deliverable: A working sandbox/permission configuration (in whatever form your actual tooling uses — a config file, a documented set of flags, a container definition) scoped explicitly across all four dimensions from lesson 2, plus a written worst-case recovery plan naming the specific failure, the specific recovery mechanism, and confirmation that the mechanism was actually tested, not just assumed to work.

stages.title: Scope the task's blast radius
stages.instructions: Write down the task in one or two sentences. Name, explicitly, which of the four access dimensions (read, write, execute, network) it genuinely needs, and which isolation level (branch, copy, container) matches its real blast radius, per lessons 2 and 3.
stages.checkpoint: All four dimensions are named explicitly with a yes/no and a reason, and the chosen isolation level is justified against the task's actual risk, not just picked by default.

stages.title: Build the actual sandbox config
stages.instructions: Configure the real isolation and permission boundary — a container, a scoped directory copy, restricted shell commands, whatever matches your actual tooling — matching exactly what stage 1 determined the task needs, no broader.
stages.checkpoint: A working configuration exists that grants exactly the scoped access from stage 1 — confirmed by actually trying an action outside that scope and seeing it get blocked.

stages.title: Identify and gate any destructive step
stages.instructions: Check the task's plan (from the previous module's decomposition skills) for any step that's destructive or hard to reverse. If one exists, write out what evidence a human confirmation on that step should surface, per lesson 4.
stages.checkpoint: Either a destructive step is identified with a real, evidence-carrying confirmation gate written for it, or a clear statement that the task genuinely has none.

stages.title: Write and test the recovery plan
stages.instructions: Name the worst plausible failure for this specific task. Identify the concrete recovery mechanism. Actually test it — restore from the backup, check the reflog, confirm the pre-run directory copy is complete and readable — before writing it up as trustworthy. Self-check against the rubric.
stages.checkpoint: The recovery plan names a specific mechanism that has been actually tested during this lab, not just described as existing.

rubric.criterion: All four access dimensions are explicitly scoped, not defaulted
rubric.meets: Read, write, execute, and network are each addressed with a yes/no and a reason tied to the specific task, including the ones scoped to 'no.'

rubric.criterion: The isolation level matches the task's real blast radius
rubric.meets: The chosen level (branch, copy, container) is justified by what the task's steps actually touch, per lesson 3's rules, not chosen for convenience in either direction.

rubric.criterion: The sandbox config actually works, confirmed by testing its boundary
rubric.meets: An action outside the intended scope was actually attempted and actually blocked, not just assumed to be blocked by the configuration's intent.

rubric.criterion: Any destructive step has a real, evidence-carrying gate
rubric.meets: If the task has a destructive step, its confirmation prompt surfaces the actual evidence behind the decision, not just the fact that a decision is pending — per lesson 4.

rubric.criterion: The recovery mechanism was actually tested, not assumed
rubric.meets: The written plan states specifically what was tried (a restore, a reflog check, a copy verification) and what it confirmed — not just that a mechanism is believed to exist.

contentSections.body: A sandbox config and a recovery plan that have both actually been tested — not just written down — are the difference between believing a task is safe and knowing what happens if it isn't.

title: Checkpoint — Tools, Files and Blast Radius
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Decomposition and Task Design (the module immediately before this one), two from Concurrency, Time and Ordering, further back in the track.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's scoping, isolation, and recovery patterns alongside earlier modules' decomposition and concurrency patterns, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Tools, Files and Blast Radius

questions.from: This module — Tools, Files and Blast Radius
questions.prompt: An agent's task description says "clean up temp files in the project," but it's been granted access to the whole home directory. What actually determines the size of a possible mistake here?

options.label: The granted access (the whole home directory), not the task's stated intent (just the project's temp files)
The task's stated intent, since that's what the agent is trying to do
Neither — the size of a mistake is unrelated to either access or intent

questions.explanation: A permission grant is a statement of possibility, not of intent — the blast radius of a mistake is bounded by what's reachable, regardless of how narrowly the task itself was described.

questions.from: This module — Tools, Files and Blast Radius
questions.prompt: Why does scoping filesystem access to read-only fail to contain the risk of an "unrestricted" shell grant sitting next to it?

options.label: Execute access isn't bounded by a filesystem path the way read/write are — a shell command can reach environment variables, the network, or paths entirely outside the scoped directory
It doesn't fail — a read-only filesystem grant fully contains whatever the shell can do
Unrestricted shell access is only a risk if the filesystem grant is also write-enabled

questions.explanation: Read and write scope to a path; execute (and network) scope to a capability that isn't naturally bounded by that path at all, and need their own explicit restriction.

questions.from: This module — Tools, Files and Blast Radius
questions.prompt: Why is a git branch, on its own, insufficient isolation for a task whose plan includes an execute step (like running an install script)?

options.label: A branch protects tracked commits from `main`; it does nothing to undo shell commands the agent ran, since those effects were never tracked by git in the first place
Branches only work for isolating a single file, not multiple files
A branch is always sufficient isolation regardless of what a task's steps do

questions.explanation: `git checkout main` reverses bad commits; it does not reverse `rm -rf`, a package's post-install script, or anything else the shell did along the way, because none of that was ever git-tracked.

questions.from: This module — Tools, Files and Blast Radius
questions.prompt: A team has a nightly backup job that has run successfully for a year with no errors. Why isn't that, on its own, a trustworthy recovery mechanism?

options.label: A backup that has never actually been restored from proves the backup process runs without erroring, not that the resulting backup can actually be restored into a working state
It is trustworthy — a year of successful runs is sufficient proof the backups work
Nightly backups are never trustworthy regardless of testing; only continuous replication counts

questions.explanation: "Runs without erroring" and "restores correctly" are different claims. Only an actual, deliberate restore test closes the gap between a scheduled job succeeding and a genuine recovery mechanism existing.

questions.from: Previous module — Decomposition and Task Design
questions.prompt: Why does breaking a large task into smaller, individually-checkable steps reduce risk compared to one large unbroken run, even when the total scope of work is identical?

options.label: Each step boundary is a point where a wrong assumption can be caught before more work is built on top of it, rather than discovered only after everything ran
Smaller steps are always individually easier to implement correctly than large ones
It doesn't reduce risk — total scope of work is what determines risk, not how it's divided

questions.explanation: The value isn't that fragments are individually easier — it's that a checkpoint between steps is a chance to catch a wrong assumption while it's still cheap to fix, before subsequent steps build on it.

questions.from: Previous module — Decomposition and Task Design
questions.prompt: What makes "done when the export feature works" a poor verification condition?

options.label: It restates the step rather than naming a specific, checkable input and output
It's phrased as a question instead of a statement
Nothing — it's a perfectly adequate verification condition

questions.explanation: A real verification condition names a concrete input and a concrete, comparable output — "works" names no observable fact anyone could check it against.

questions.from: Previous module — Decomposition and Task Design
questions.prompt: Why should a plan's one destructive step generally be placed last, rather than wherever it fits most naturally by task logic?

options.label: Because it's hard or impossible to reverse, so every step that might reveal a wrong assumption should run first, while reversing is still cheap
Destructive steps are always the fastest to execute, so doing them last saves no real time either way
It should generally be placed first, to get the risky part out of the way early

questions.explanation: Reversible steps first, destructive last — every step that could surface a wrong assumption gets the chance to do so while undoing it still just means not running the next step.

questions.from: Previous module — Decomposition and Task Design
questions.prompt: A plan step reads: "decide whether to grandfather existing customers at the old price." Why does this need a human checkpoint despite being written in the same flat style as the mechanical steps around it?

options.label: Its correct answer depends on a business tradeoff outside the codebase, not something the code alone determines
It doesn't — any step phrased as a clear instruction is safe for an agent to run unattended
Only steps involving payment processing ever need a checkpoint

questions.explanation: The test for a judgment step is whether the inputs alone determine one correct answer, not its wording or subject matter — a pricing/policy tradeoff depends on information the code has no access to.

questions.from: Three modules back — Concurrency, Time and Ordering
questions.prompt: Two requests hit the same record at nearly the same time: both read the current value, both compute an update based on what they read, both write. What's the resulting risk called, and why does it happen?

options.label: A lost update — the second write overwrites the first because both reads happened before either write, so neither request saw the other's change
A deadlock — neither request can proceed because each is waiting on the other
This isn't actually a risk as long as both requests eventually complete successfully

questions.explanation: A read-then-write pattern with no locking or atomic update lets two concurrent requests both read the same starting value, compute independently, and have the second write silently clobber the first — the update one of them intended is simply lost, with no error raised anywhere.

questions.from: Three modules back — Concurrency, Time and Ordering
questions.prompt: A payment retry fires because the first response timed out, but the first charge actually succeeded on the provider's side before the timeout. Without an idempotency key, what happens?

options.label: The customer is charged twice, because the retry has no way to tell the provider "this is a repeat of a request that may have already succeeded"
The provider automatically detects and rejects the duplicate charge with no extra work required
The retry is safe by default as long as it uses the same request body as the original

questions.explanation: A timeout tells you the response was lost, not that the operation failed — retrying blindly risks re-executing an action that already succeeded. An idempotency key lets the provider recognize a retried request as the same logical operation rather than a new one, which a merely-identical request body does not guarantee on its own.

title: "Done" is a claim, not a result
description: Why an agent's own report that a task succeeded is evidence to check, not a result to accept — and what it means that the summary and the mistake can come from the same source.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an agent's completion summary is a claim requiring verification, not a verified result
Identify when a report of success is being trusted without any independent check behind it

contentSections.title: The summary and the mistake share an author

contentSections.body: "Migration complete — all 340 rows backfilled, tests passing." You move on to the next task. Two days later a support ticket comes in: a customer's order history is missing entries from before the migration. You go back and actually run the migration's own verification query yourself: 337 rows, not 340. Three silently didn't backfill — a constraint violation on three rows with a null field, caught by a try/except inside the migration script that logged a warning and moved on, in a log file nobody read because the final line printed "complete." The agent didn't lie. It reported exactly what it believed to be true, based on exactly the same reasoning that produced the gap in the first place.

A completion report is generated by the same process that did the work — which means whatever assumption, blind spot, or misreading caused a step to go wrong is available to color the report of that step just as easily as it colored the step itself. This isn't a claim that agents are dishonest; it's a structural fact about self-reporting that applies to a careful human summarizing their own work, too. If the migration script's own logic believed 340 rows meant success, the report built from that same logic will say success, because from the inside, nothing looked wrong.

The practical consequence is not "never trust an agent's summary" — a summary is genuinely useful as a map of what was attempted and where to look. It's that a summary of success functions as a claim, and a claim needs something independent of the process that produced it to check it against: the actual row count, the actual test output, the actual file contents — not a restatement of the same report in different words.

contentSections.scenario: An agent runs a data-cleanup script and reports: "Cleaned up 1,204 duplicate records, verified no data loss." The verification step it performed: re-running its own cleanup script's summary logic, which counts how many records its own deletion logic identified as duplicates, and confirms that number matches what it deleted.
contentSections.question: Why doesn't this "verification" actually verify anything meaningful?

options.label: The check re-uses the exact same logic that identified the duplicates in the first place — if that logic was wrong about what counts as a duplicate, the check confirms the wrong count consistently rather than catching the error
1,204 is suspiciously low for a real cleanup and should have been higher
The main problem is that the script didn't log each individual deletion for audit purposes

feedback.same-logic: Right. A check that shares its logic with the thing it's checking can only ever confirm internal consistency — "I deleted what I identified" — never correctness — "what I identified was actually correct." If the duplicate-detection logic had a flawed comparison (say, treating two genuinely distinct records with a shared email typo as duplicates), this verification would confirm that mistake with complete confidence.
feedback.count-too-low: There's no way to judge whether 1,204 is a plausible count without knowing the dataset — and even a perfectly plausible number doesn't tell you whether the *records themselves* were correctly identified as duplicates. The number isn't the problem; the method behind it is.
feedback.should-have-logged: Better logging would help someone investigate after the fact, but it doesn't make the verification step itself any more independent — the underlying issue is that nothing outside the cleanup's own logic checked its own logic.

contentSections.mechanism: A verification step only verifies something if it's independent of the process being checked — built on a different basis than the thing it's confirming. A count that re-derives from the same duplicate-detection logic that made the deletions is not an independent check; it's the same reasoning, run twice, guaranteed to agree with itself.

contentSections.body: A claim of success generated by the same process that did the work can be wrong in exactly the same way the work was — check it against something independent, not against a restatement of itself.

contentSections.title: "Trust but verify" undersells it

contentSections.body:
"Trust but verify" implies trust is the default state and verification is an occasional audit layered on top. For agent work specifically, this framing has the weight backwards: an unverified claim of success carries roughly the same evidentiary value as an unverified claim of failure — which is to say, some, but not enough to act on for anything that matters. The claim is a starting point for an investigation, not the conclusion of one.

This doesn't mean re-verifying everything with equal intensity — the rest of this module is largely about making that verification cheap and proportionate, not about turning every step into a full audit. It means the default mental model shifts from "the agent said it worked, so it probably did" to "the agent said it worked — here's what I'd check to actually know." Sometimes that check is fast (l5's cheap checks). Sometimes, for something with real stakes, it's a full independent verification (l4). What it's never allowed to be is skipped because the summary sounded confident.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: is an unverified claim of task success more trustworthy than an unverified claim of task failure, less trustworthy, or roughly the same?
contentSections.answer: Roughly the same — neither has been checked against anything independent yet, so both are a starting point for investigation rather than a conclusion. The confidence of the wording doesn't change that.
contentSections.hint: Ask what evidence actually backs either claim before anyone has gone and checked something real.

contentSections.body: An unverified success claim and an unverified failure claim carry roughly the same evidentiary weight — neither is a conclusion, both are a starting point for a check.

title: Reading a run log for what was skipped
description: The specific tells in a transcript — a caught exception, a silent fallback, a truncated read, a phrase like "I'll assume" — that mark a place where something was skipped rather than done.

learningObjectives.text: Identify specific textual and structural tells in an agent transcript that indicate a step was skipped, assumed, or worked around rather than completed

contentSections.title: The transcript already told you — you just didn't scan for it

contentSections.body: The transcript of the row-backfill migration from lesson 1, read end to end rather than just its last line, contains this, buried between two much longer sections about the parts that went smoothly: "Encountered 3 rows with null `region` field, which the mapping function doesn't handle — caught the exception and skipped these rows to allow the rest of the batch to complete." That sentence was there the whole time. Nobody read the whole transcript; they read the final summary, which described the batch as complete without repeating the one line that qualified it.

A run log almost always contains the information needed to catch a silent partial failure — the problem is rarely that the information is missing, it's that a transcript can run to hundreds of lines and the one sentence that matters looks structurally identical to the surrounding ones that don't. Reading for what was skipped means scanning specifically for a small set of recurring tells, rather than reading the whole thing start to finish hoping something jumps out.

The recurring tells: a caught exception followed by continuation ("caught the error and skipped/continued/moved on"), a silent fallback ("couldn't find X, using default Y instead" — without flagging that the default might be wrong for this case), a truncated or partial read (a file read that stopped at a line limit, a paginated API call that only fetched the first page), and a hedge phrase ("I'll assume," "this should," "presumably" — language marking a decision made without confirmation). None of these are necessarily catastrophic on their own. Each one is a place worth a second look before trusting the summary that follows it.

contentSections.code:
Transcript excerpt from an agent updating a reporting dashboard's data pipeline:

"Updated the aggregation query to include the new `region` field. Ran the pipeline against last month's data — output looked reasonable. Note: the pipeline normally validates row counts against the source table before publishing, but that validation step timed out against this month's larger dataset, so I published without it. Dashboard is now live with the updated field."
contentSections.question: What's the actual problem hiding in this otherwise routine-sounding update?

options.label: The validation step — the one specifically designed to catch a bad row count — was skipped, and the pipeline published anyway, with the skip mentioned only in passing after the fact
The new `region` field itself is described incorrectly and likely has a bug
"Output looked reasonable" is sufficient confirmation that the update is correct

feedback.skipped-validation: Right. The pipeline has a real, specific safety check built for exactly this kind of change, and it didn't run — not because it failed, but because it timed out and the run proceeded to publish anyway. This is the tell to catch: a designed safeguard being bypassed reads, in this transcript, exactly like a minor operational note rather than the headline it actually is.
feedback.region-field-wrong: There's no evidence in this transcript that the field itself is wrong — the actual issue is that the one mechanism that would have caught a row-count problem, whether or not the field itself has a bug, didn't run.
feedback.output-looked-reasonable: "Looked reasonable" is a subjective, unquantified impression — it's exactly the kind of language this lesson flags as a hedge, standing in for the actual validation that didn't happen.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This is the truncated/skipped-validation tell in its most common real shape: a genuine safety mechanism existed, it didn't run due to an operational issue (a timeout, not a design flaw), and the run proceeded anyway with the omission noted in passing rather than flagged as blocking. The fix isn't necessarily "never publish without validation" — it's that this exact situation needed a stop-and-ask moment, not a quiet continue-and-mention-it-later.

contentSections.body: Scan a transcript specifically for caught exceptions, silent fallbacks, truncated reads, and hedge phrases — the information is usually already there, just not where the final summary line points.

contentSections.title: A skip isn't automatically a failure to catch

contentSections.body:
Not every tell from the first half of this lesson means something went wrong — some skips are genuinely fine, and treating every hedge phrase as an emergency is its own failure mode, one that makes the actually useful signal harder to hear amid constant false alarms. "Couldn't find a `CHANGELOG.md`, so I didn't update one" is a skip that's almost certainly a non-issue if the project never had one. The distinction that matters: was the skipped thing something the task actually depended on, or something genuinely incidental to it?

The practical test: for each tell found, ask "does anything downstream of this assume the skipped thing happened correctly?" The three null-region rows in the migration mattered because customer-facing order history depended on all 340 rows being present. A missing changelog update rarely has anything built on top of it. Reading a transcript well isn't about flagging every hedge — it's about tracing which flagged hedges have real weight resting on them.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what's the one test that separates a tell worth investigating from a tell that's genuinely low-stakes?
contentSections.answer: Whether anything downstream depends on the skipped thing having happened correctly — a skip nothing is built on top of is low-stakes; a skip real logic or real data depends on is worth investigating regardless of how minor it sounds in the transcript.
contentSections.hint: It isn't about how alarming the phrase sounds — it's about what, if anything, relies on the skipped thing being right.

contentSections.body: For every tell you catch, ask whether anything downstream actually depends on the skipped thing having happened correctly — that's what separates a real gap from noise.

title: The step that silently failed and the four built on top of it
description: Why a single unnoticed failure early in a chain doesn't stay contained to that step — and how to trace a downstream symptom back to the step where it actually started.

learningObjectives.text: Trace a downstream failure symptom back to the earliest step in a chain where the underlying problem actually originated
Explain why a silent failure compounds in cost the further downstream it travels before being caught

contentSections.title: One silent exit code, four steps built on top of it

contentSections.body: A five-step deploy chain: (1) run the build, (2) run the test suite against the build, (3) push the build to staging, (4) run a smoke test against staging, (5) promote to production. The transcript shows all five steps completing. Production is now serving a build from three days ago. What happened: step 1's build script hit a warning-level lint error, printed the warning, and exited 0 anyway — a caught, non-fatal condition. Step 2's test suite ran, correctly, against the newly built artifact — but the build artifact from step 1 was actually the *previous* successful build, because the current build step, despite exiting 0, had failed to overwrite the output directory due to a stale file lock the lint warning was actually about. Steps 2 through 5 all "succeeded," truthfully, against a build that was never the current one.

A silent failure in step 1 didn't just fail to be caught — it changed what "success" meant for every step after it. Step 2 wasn't lying when it reported tests passing; it genuinely ran the suite and the suite genuinely passed, against an artifact that simply wasn't the one anyone intended. This is what makes chain failures expensive to diagnose after the fact: by the time a symptom appears (production running stale code), four steps of accurate, honestly-reported success sit between the observer and the one step where things actually went wrong.

The cost of a silent failure scales with how far downstream it travels before detection, for the same reason this was true of decomposition and ordering earlier in this track: every step built on top of the bad assumption inherits it, and the diagnostic work to find the origin grows with each additional step, because each one now has to be individually ruled out as the actual source before the search can move further back.

contentSections.scenario: The deploy chain above, investigated after the fact. A responder notices production is stale and starts investigating at step 5 (the promotion step), confirms it correctly promoted whatever was in staging, then checks step 4 (the smoke test), confirms it correctly tested what was in staging, then checks step 3 (the push to staging), confirms it correctly pushed whatever step 1 produced.
contentSections.question: Which direction should this investigation actually run, and why?

options.label: Backward from the symptom toward the earliest step, exactly as shown — each step is individually confirmed correct given its own input, which pushes the search further back until the step whose *input* was already wrong is found
Forward from step 1, since that's always the correct place to start any investigation
It doesn't matter which direction, since all five steps will need to be checked regardless

feedback.backward-from-symptom: Right — and this is exactly what's shown happening. Each step downstream of the real problem did its own job correctly given what it was handed; the failure isn't in any of their logic, it's in what they were given to work with. Tracing backward from the symptom, confirming each step's own correctness given its input, is what eventually lands on step 1 — the first place where a step's *output* doesn't match what it should have been.
feedback.forward-from-start: Starting at step 1 isn't wrong, exactly, but it isn't always necessary either — if the earlier steps of a long chain have independent evidence they worked (a previous, unrelated run confirmed them, for instance), backward tracing from the symptom can localize the problem faster without redoing already-confirmed work.
feedback.doesn't-matter: Direction changes how much unnecessary re-checking happens. Backward tracing from the symptom can, in principle, stop as soon as a step's output is found to not match its downstream steps' assumption — it doesn't require re-verifying steps that independent evidence already covers.

contentSections.mechanism: In a chain where each step's correctness is defined relative to its own input, a downstream failure investigation should trace backward: confirm each step behaved correctly given what it received, and the moment a step's *received input* is found to not match what it should have been, the problem is one step further back than where the symptom appeared.

contentSections.body: A downstream symptom rarely marks where the problem started — trace backward from the symptom, confirming each step's correctness relative to what it actually received, until a step's input itself is the thing that's wrong.

contentSections.title: This is why per-step verification exists at all

contentSections.body:
The deploy chain example is the concrete cost this whole module is built to prevent — not because a smarter agent would have caught the stale build lock, but because the entire failure was invisible to every check that only looked at each step's own claimed exit status. `exit 0` was, in a narrow sense, true. What was missing was any check that confirmed the build step's *actual output* — the artifact itself — matched what a fresh build should look like, independent of what the build script itself reported about its own exit code.

This reframes what per-step verification is actually protecting against: not primarily an agent lying about what it did, but an agent (or a script, or a person) honestly reporting a locally-true fact that no longer means what everyone assumed it meant. Checking the artifact — did the build output's timestamp actually update, does it contain the change that was supposed to be in it — closes exactly the gap that exit-code-only checking leaves open, and is the direct subject of the next lesson.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: what did the deploy-chain failure's own per-step checking actually protect against, and what did it fail to catch?
contentSections.answer: It protected against each step behaving incorrectly relative to what it received — every step did that correctly. It failed to catch the case where a step honestly reported a locally-true fact (exit 0) that no longer meant what everyone assumed (a fresh artifact) — only checking the actual output, not the exit code, closes that gap.
contentSections.hint: The steps weren't lying — think about what an honest, locally-true report can still fail to guarantee.

contentSections.body: A local, honestly-reported success at one step can still mean the wrong thing if what it was checking wasn't actually what mattered — checking the artifact itself is what closes that gap.

title: Independent verification: checking the artefact, not the transcript
description: Verifying a step by inspecting what it actually produced — the file, the diff, the database row, the deployed artifact — rather than by re-reading what the agent said it produced.

learningObjectives.text: Verify a completed step by inspecting its actual produced artefact rather than its narration of what it produced

contentSections.title: The transcript and the artefact are different sources of truth

contentSections.body: "Added input validation to the signup form — rejects empty emails and short passwords, tested and working." Two ways to check this. First: read that sentence again, notice it sounds specific and confident, move on. Second: actually POST an empty email to the signup endpoint and look at the response. The second one takes forty seconds. It's also the only one of the two that can actually tell you whether the claim is true — the first one just confirms the sentence exists.

The transcript is a record of what the agent did and believed happened. The artefact — the file on disk, the actual HTTP response, the row in the database, the running process — is what actually exists as a result. These are supposed to agree, and usually do, but the entire value of independent verification comes from the cases where they don't, and reading the transcript more carefully will never catch a case where the transcript itself is what's wrong or incomplete, the way step 1's exit code was in the previous lesson.

Checking the artefact means going around the agent's own account entirely: run the actual request, read the actual file, query the actual table, diff the actual output against a known-good reference. This isn't slower distrust for its own sake — for most steps, it's a very short, specific action, exactly the kind this module's earlier lessons on transcripts and chains were building toward being able to target precisely instead of needing to check everything with equal effort.

contentSections.scenario: Five ways a reviewer might "confirm" the signup-validation step above actually works.
contentSections.question: Select every method below that constitutes real, independent verification — checking the artefact, not the transcript.

items.label: Re-reading the agent's summary a second time to make sure it sounds confident and specific
Sending an actual POST request with an empty email and checking the real HTTP response code and body
Asking the agent to explain, in more detail, how the validation logic works
Reading the actual diff and confirming the validation code checks for both conditions the task specified
Running the project's existing test suite and confirming a new test for empty-email rejection is present and passing

explanation.s1: This never leaves the transcript — a more careful re-read of the same claim produces the same claim, not new information.
explanation.s2: This is exactly the artefact check: a real request against the real system, producing a real, independently-observed result.
explanation.s3: More explanation from the same source that made the original claim is still that same source — it can produce a more detailed wrong answer just as easily as a more detailed correct one.
explanation.s4: Reading the actual diff (not a description of the diff) is checking the real artefact — the code itself, not a summary of the code.
explanation.s5: A passing, actually-executed test that specifically covers the claimed behavior is a genuine independent check — provided the test itself is confirmed to actually test the right thing, not just that some test with a plausible name exists.

contentSections.body: Asking for more explanation from the same source that made a claim isn't verification — it's the same claim, restated. Verification means going around the source entirely to check the actual artefact.

contentSections.title: Choosing which artefact actually matters

contentSections.body:
Not every artefact is equally informative, and checking the wrong one produces the same false confidence as not checking at all. For the deploy-chain failure two lessons back, checking "did step 2's test suite pass" was checking a real artefact (real test output) — and it still missed the problem, because the test suite's own artefact (a pass/fail result) didn't encode the one fact that actually mattered: which build artifact it had run against. The lesson isn't just "check something real" — it's checking the specific real thing the task's verification condition (from the earlier decomposition module) actually named.

This is where the earlier module's habit of writing verification conditions before a step runs pays off directly: a condition written as "a POST with an empty email returns 400" tells you exactly which artefact to check afterward — the HTTP response. A vague step with no real verification condition leaves you guessing which artefact would even be informative, after the fact, which is a much harder question to answer well than deciding it in advance.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: the deploy chain's step 2 checked a real artefact (actual test output) and still missed the problem. Why?
contentSections.answer: The test output was real, but it didn't encode the one fact that actually mattered — which build artifact the tests had run against. Checking a real artefact only helps if it's the artefact that would actually reveal the specific thing at risk.
contentSections.hint: Being real isn't the same as being informative about the specific risk — what did the test result actually confirm, and what did it stay silent about?

contentSections.body: A verification condition written before a step runs is what tells you, afterward, exactly which real artefact to go check — guessing which one matters after the fact is a much harder problem.

title: Cheap checks you can run after every step
description: Building a small set of fast, low-effort checks — a diff line count, a grep for a specific pattern, an exit code combined with an output check — that catch most silent failures without a full audit on every single step.

learningObjectives.text: Design a fast, cheap verification check appropriate to a step's specific risk, run as default hygiene rather than a full audit

contentSections.title: Not everything needs the forty-second version

contentSections.body: A full independent verification — the artefact check from the previous lesson — takes real time and attention, which is exactly right for a step with real stakes and exactly wrong as a default for all forty steps in a long, low-risk run. A cheap check doesn't replace a full verification where one's warranted; it catches most of the same silent failures at a fraction of the cost, for the many steps where a full audit would be overkill. `git diff --stat` after a step that was supposed to touch three files takes one second and immediately tells you if it touched thirty instead, or zero.

Cheap checks share a shape: fast, automatable, and aimed at a specific, common failure signature rather than a general "is this correct" question. A diff-stat check catches a step that touched far more or far fewer files than expected — the shape of both the runaway-scope failure and the silently-skipped-work failure from earlier lessons. A grep for `TODO`, `FIXME`, or `pass  # stub` catches an agent that left a placeholder where real logic was supposed to go. Checking an exit code *and* the actual line count of an output file (not just the exit code alone) catches the deploy-chain failure's exact shape — a script that exits 0 without having produced what it should have.

None of these are substitutes for the artefact check when a step genuinely warrants one. They're a first line, run by default, cheap enough that skipping them has no real justification — and specifically designed to catch the failure modes this module has spent four lessons naming, in seconds rather than minutes.

contentSections.problem: Design cheap checks for a step: "remove the deprecated `legacy_search` function and its three call sites, replacing them with `search_v2`."

steps.label: Check the diff shape matches the expected scope
steps.work: `git diff --stat` should show changes in roughly four places: the file defining `legacy_search` and the three call-site files. Zero files changed, or one file changed, is an immediate red flag before reading a single line.
steps.why: This catches both extremes cheaply: a step that did nothing (0 files) and a step whose scope quietly grew far beyond the three named call sites.

steps.label: Grep for the old name to confirm it's actually gone, not just partially replaced
steps.work: `grep -rn "legacy_search" .` after the change should return nothing (or only a changelog/comment mentioning it historically) — if it still returns hits in code, at least one call site was missed.
steps.why: The step's own claim of 'replacing all three call sites' is exactly the kind of count-based claim that's cheap and fast to check directly, rather than trusting the transcript's count.

steps.label: Grep for stub or placeholder markers in the new code
steps.work: `grep -n "TODO\|FIXME\|pass  # " <changed files>` catches a `search_v2` call site that was swapped in as a stub rather than a real replacement.
steps.why: A common shortcut under time pressure (real or simulated) is leaving a placeholder with the intent to fill it in later — this check catches that shortcut before it's mistaken for done.

faded.problem: Design cheap checks for a step: "add a new required `sku` field to the product creation API, with validation rejecting requests missing it."

blanks.prompt: What's a cheap diff-shape check for this step?
blanks.answer: `git diff --stat` should show the product-creation handler and its validation schema/logic changing — a change that touches only one of the two, or neither, suggests the validation half or the field-addition half was skipped.
accept: diff stat should show both the handler and the validation logic changed
blanks.why: Two distinct pieces of work were described (add the field, add the validation) — a diff shape covering only one is a cheap signal that the other might be missing.

blanks.prompt: What's a cheap, direct check (not reading the diff) that actually tests the claimed behavior?
blanks.answer: Send an actual POST request to the product-creation endpoint with no `sku` field and check that the response is a 400/422, not a 200 or 500.
accept: send a real request missing sku and check for a rejection status code
blanks.why: This is the artefact check from the previous lesson, made cheap — a single request takes seconds and directly tests the one behavior the step was supposed to add, rather than trusting a diff read alone.

blanks.prompt: What's a cheap grep-based check for a common shortcut on this kind of step?
blanks.answer: `grep -n "sku" <validation file>` to confirm the field is actually referenced in the validation logic, not just added to a schema definition with no enforcement wired to it.
accept: grep for the field name in the validation logic to confirm it's actually enforced there
blanks.why: A field can be added to a schema/type definition without ever being checked at request time — this is the same 'looks complete, isn't wired up' failure from earlier in the track, and a one-line grep catches it fast.

contentSections.procedure: For any step: check the diff shape against the expected scope, grep for the specific claim the step made (a name removed, a field added) to confirm it directly rather than trusting the count in the summary, and grep for stub/placeholder markers in whatever was newly added.

contentSections.body: A cheap check aimed at a specific failure shape — diff scope, a name that should be gone, a placeholder that shouldn't be there — catches most silent failures in seconds, as a default, without needing a full audit on every step.

contentSections.title: Cheap checks are a floor, not a ceiling

contentSections.body:
The risk in this lesson's own framing is treating "I ran a cheap check" as equivalent to "I verified this step," the same substitution this whole module has been warning against in other forms. A cheap check is a fast, high-value floor — run it on everything, by default, because the cost of doing so is close to zero. It is not a substitute for the full artefact check from the previous lesson on a step where the stakes actually warrant one, any more than a smoke detector is a substitute for a fire inspector on the step that's actually carrying real risk.

The two aren't in tension; they're stacked. Cheap checks run on every step, cheaply, catching the common shapes of silent failure by default. A full independent verification runs on the steps this module's earlier lessons would flag as high-stakes, destructive, or otherwise deserving of it. Knowing which is which — a judgment call this whole module has been building toward — is itself the skill, not a fixed rule for every situation.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: would a diff-stat or a TODO-grep have caught the deploy-chain's stale-build failure from lesson 3?
contentSections.answer: No — the diff shape and content looked entirely normal; nothing in that failure resembled a scope mismatch or a leftover placeholder. This is exactly why cheap checks are a floor, not a replacement for a full artefact check on steps with real stakes.
contentSections.hint: Think back to what specifically went wrong in that failure, and whether either cheap-check pattern would have any reason to flag it.

contentSections.body: Cheap checks are a floor run on everything by default — they don't replace a full artefact check on the steps that genuinely warrant one.

contentSections.title: One good run proves nothing

contentSections.body:
Everything so far in this lesson is a check on one result. There is a second check, and it costs a little more: run the same brief several times and compare.

If you ask an agent for the same small piece of work three to five times, the answers will not be identical. That is not a defect to complain about. It is information. Where the runs differ, one of two things is true. Either the brief left something unsaid, so the agent filled the gap differently each time. Or the task has a genuinely hard part that the agent handles inconsistently.

Where all the runs agree, be careful. Agreement tells you the result is consistent. It does not tell you it is correct. Five runs can share the same wrong assumption.

Do this on a small slice of the work, not the whole project. Five runs cost five times as much, so spend them on the part you are least sure of. On a low-energy day, three runs and a one-line note on what differed is enough.

contentSections.scenario: You give an agent the same brief five times: "Write a function that turns a list of order lines into a total including VAT." Run 1 rounds each line and then adds them up. Run 2 adds them up and then rounds once. Runs 3 and 5 match run 1. Run 4 matches run 1 but never handles a line with quantity zero. Run 2 finished faster than the others.
contentSections.question: Select every observation that tells you something about the brief, not only about the agent.

items.label: Runs 1 and 2 round at different points
Run 4 skips the zero-quantity case that the others handled
Runs 1, 3 and 5 produced the same code, so that approach must be right
Run 2 was faster than the others

explanation.rounding: The brief never said when to round, so the agent chose differently. Money totals change by a cent depending on the answer. This is a gap in your brief that you can close in one sentence.
explanation.zero: A case that only some runs handle is a case the brief did not mention. Decide what should happen with a zero quantity, write it down, and the difference disappears.
explanation.agree: Three runs agreeing shows consistency, not correctness. They may all round each line first because that is the common habit, which may or may not match what your accounts need. Check the answer against a worked example, not against the other runs.
explanation.speed: Speed tells you nothing about whether the brief was clear. It is the easiest thing to see and the least useful.

contentSections.body: Where five runs of the same brief disagree, the brief left something unsaid. Where they all agree, you have consistency, which is not the same as correct.

title: Audit eight run logs for unverified claims
description: Eight drills, no new concepts: given a transcript excerpt, find the unverified claim, the skipped step, or the artefact that would actually confirm or disprove it.

learningObjectives.text: Apply transcript-reading, chain-tracing, and artefact-verification skills at speed against unfamiliar run logs

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills against real-shaped run logs, in no particular order of difficulty — done in one sitting or spread out, nothing here expires.
If a drill needed the hint before the unverified claim jumped out, that's the tell worth watching for in your own next transcript.

title: Verify an agent run end to end against its own plan
description: Take a real agent run you actually did (or a genuine one you run for this lab), and verify every one of its steps independently against the artefact — not the transcript — producing a full verification report.

learningObjectives.text: Independently verify every step of a real multi-step agent run against its actual artefact
Produce a verification report marking each step done, partial, or not done, with concrete evidence for the marking

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every failure this module used was already found and diagnosed for you. This lab closes that gap: take a real multi-step agent run — ideally one you actually did for this track's earlier labs, or a fresh genuine one — and verify every single step yourself, against the real artefact, writing down what you actually find.

contentSections.title: Verify an agent run end to end against its own plan
contentSections.brief: Take a real multi-step agent run with a written plan behind it (reuse one from this phase's earlier labs if you have one, or run a fresh multi-step task with a plan first). For every step in the plan, independently verify what actually happened — check the real artefact, not the transcript's account of it — and mark it done, partial, or not done, with the specific evidence behind that marking.
contentSections.deliverable: A verification report: one entry per planned step, each marked done/partial/not-done, each with the specific artefact check performed and its actual result (not a restatement of what the transcript claimed). At least one entry should use a cheap check from lesson 5; at least one should use a full independent artefact check from lesson 4.

stages.title: Gather the plan and the run
stages.instructions: Lay the original step plan and the actual run transcript side by side. Note, before checking anything, any tells from lesson 2 (caught exceptions, hedge phrases, silent fallbacks) visible just from a first read of the transcript.
stages.checkpoint: The plan and transcript are both in hand, and an initial list of textual tells worth investigating exists before any artefact checking starts.

stages.title: Verify each step against its real artefact
stages.instructions: For every planned step, perform the actual check — run the request, read the actual diff, query the actual data, check the actual file — not a re-read of the transcript's account of it. Use a cheap check where the step's stakes are low, a full artefact check where they're higher, per lessons 4 and 5. Write down exactly what was checked and what it showed.
stages.checkpoint: Every step has an independent, artefact-based check performed and recorded — not inferred from the transcript alone.

stages.title: Write the report and self-check
stages.instructions: Compile the verification report: one line per step, its done/partial/not-done marking, and the specific evidence. If anything came back partial or not-done, note what it would take to actually finish it. Self-check against the rubric.
stages.checkpoint: A complete report exists covering every step in the original plan, each with concrete evidence, not a restated summary.

rubric.criterion: Every planned step has an entry in the report
rubric.meets: No step from the original plan is missing from the report, including any that turn out to be genuinely, fully done — a clean result is a legitimate, useful entry too.

rubric.criterion: Each marking is backed by an independently-checked artefact, not the transcript
rubric.meets: The evidence named for each entry is something actually checked outside the agent's own narration — a real request, a real diff, a real query result — not a more careful reading of what the agent said.

rubric.criterion: At least one entry uses a cheap check and at least one uses a full artefact check
rubric.meets: The report shows the proportionate judgment from lesson 5 — not every step got the same depth of check, and the choice of depth is defensible given each step's actual stakes.

rubric.criterion: Any partial or not-done finding traces to a specific cause
rubric.meets: A step marked partial or not-done names what specifically was missing or wrong, in the same concrete terms lesson 3's backward-tracing skill used — not a vague 'something's off here.'

rubric.criterion: The report is usable as a real handoff document
rubric.meets: Someone else could read this report and know exactly what's actually finished, what isn't, and what evidence backs each claim — without needing the original transcript in front of them.

contentSections.body: A verification report that names the actual artefact checked for every step is worth more than a completion summary that sounds confident — it's the difference between believing a run succeeded and knowing which parts of it did.

title: Checkpoint — Verifying a Chain, Not a Completion
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Tools, Files and Blast Radius (the module immediately before this one), two from Error Handling and Failure Paths, further back in the track.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's claim-checking and artefact-verification patterns alongside earlier modules' scoping and failure-handling patterns, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Verifying a Chain, Not a Completion

questions.from: This module — Verifying a Chain, Not a Completion
questions.prompt: A data-cleanup script's "verification" step re-runs its own duplicate-detection logic and confirms the count matches what it deleted. Why doesn't this actually verify anything?

options.label: It shares its logic with the process being checked, so it can only confirm internal consistency, never correctness — a flawed detection rule would pass this check with full confidence
It doesn't check enough records to be statistically meaningful
It's actually a valid, sufficient verification

questions.explanation: A check built on the same logic as the thing it checks can only confirm the process agreed with itself — never that the underlying logic was correct in the first place.

questions.from: This module — Verifying a Chain, Not a Completion
questions.prompt: A five-step deploy chain reports every step successful, but production ends up serving a stale build. Where did the investigation need to trace, and why?

options.label: Backward from the symptom, confirming each step's correctness relative to its own input, until a step's received input is itself found to be wrong
Nowhere — if every step reported success, the reported success is sufficient and the symptom must be unrelated
Only the final step needs investigating, since that's where the symptom appeared

questions.explanation: Each downstream step performed correctly given what it received — the actual problem was one step further back, where the *output* first diverged from what it should have been, which only backward tracing from the symptom finds efficiently.

questions.from: This module — Verifying a Chain, Not a Completion
questions.prompt: Why does asking an agent to "explain in more detail how the validation works" fail as independent verification of a claimed fix?

options.label: It's still the same source that made the original claim — a more detailed answer from that source can be just as wrong as the original claim, without adding any new, independent information
It doesn't fail — a sufficiently detailed explanation is equivalent to checking the artefact
It fails only because agents are generally bad at giving detailed explanations

questions.explanation: Verification requires going around the original source to check something independent — the real request, the real diff, the real output — not asking the same source to elaborate on its own claim.

questions.from: This module — Verifying a Chain, Not a Completion
questions.prompt: Why are cheap checks (a diff-stat, a grep for a removed name) a floor rather than a full replacement for independent artefact verification?

options.label: They catch common, cheap-to-detect failure shapes by default, but a step with real stakes still needs the deeper, artefact-specific check a cheap pattern-match can't provide
They aren't a floor — a cheap check is exactly as thorough as a full verification
Cheap checks should be avoided entirely in favor of always running the full verification

questions.explanation: The two are stacked, not interchangeable — cheap checks run on everything by default at near-zero cost, while high-stakes steps still warrant the deeper, specific artefact check cheap pattern-matching can't substitute for.

questions.from: Previous module — Tools, Files and Blast Radius
questions.prompt: An agent's task description says "clean up temp files in the project," but it's been granted access to the whole home directory. What determines the size of a possible mistake here?

options.label: The granted access (the whole home directory), not the task's stated intent
The task's stated intent, since that's what the agent is trying to do
Neither — mistake size is unrelated to access or intent

questions.explanation: A permission grant is a statement of possibility, not of intent — blast radius is bounded by what's reachable, regardless of how narrowly a task was described.

questions.from: Previous module — Tools, Files and Blast Radius
questions.prompt: Why does scoping filesystem access to read-only fail to contain an "unrestricted" shell grant sitting next to it?

options.label: Execute access isn't bounded by a filesystem path — a shell command can reach environment variables, the network, or paths entirely outside the scoped directory
It doesn't fail — read-only filesystem access fully contains whatever the shell can do
Unrestricted shell access only matters if the filesystem grant is also write-enabled

questions.explanation: Read and write scope to a path; execute (and network) scope to a capability that isn't naturally bounded by that path, and need their own explicit restriction.

questions.from: Previous module — Tools, Files and Blast Radius
questions.prompt: Why is a git branch, on its own, insufficient isolation for a task whose plan includes an execute step?

options.label: A branch protects tracked commits from `main`; it does nothing to undo shell commands the agent ran, since those effects were never git-tracked in the first place
Branches only isolate a single file at a time
A branch is always sufficient isolation regardless of a task's steps

questions.explanation: `git checkout main` reverses bad commits, not `rm -rf` or a package's post-install script — none of that was ever git-tracked.

questions.from: Previous module — Tools, Files and Blast Radius
questions.prompt: Why is a bare "about to delete this table — confirm?" prompt a weak gate on a destructive operation?

options.label: It gives the person answering nothing to evaluate beyond the agent's own claim that it's fine, so a quick 'yes' functions as a rubber stamp, not a real check
It's a strong gate — the mere presence of a confirmation step is sufficient protection
It's weak only because it doesn't require typing the table name to confirm

questions.explanation: A real gate surfaces the evidence behind a decision — what was checked, and what it doesn't cover — not just the fact that a decision is pending.

questions.from: Three modules back — Error Handling and Failure Paths
questions.prompt: A multi-step signup writes a user row, then a workspace row, then calls a billing API — and the billing call fails partway through. What does 'partial failure' mean here?

options.label: The user and workspace rows already committed and now exist with no corresponding billing record, unless something explicitly detects and repairs that state
The entire operation automatically rolls back across all three steps, including the external billing call
Partial failure only matters if the billing API returns a 500 rather than timing out

questions.explanation: A database transaction, if one is even in play, only covers database operations — it has no power to undo an external API call, so a failure partway through leaves earlier committed steps in place with nothing to reconcile them automatically.

questions.from: Three modules back — Error Handling and Failure Paths
questions.prompt: What can the caller of a function actually do differently if a swallowed error returns `null` for every distinct failure type, versus if the specific error were preserved?

options.label: With the specific error preserved, the caller can distinguish a retryable failure (a timeout) from a permanent one (a 404) and respond appropriately; with everything collapsed to null, it can only treat every failure identically
Nothing — a caller can't meaningfully act on error information regardless of how it's represented
The caller can always infer the specific failure type from context, regardless of what the function returns

questions.explanation: Preserving the specific failure (a timeout versus a not-found versus a validation error) is what lets a caller retry, surface a real message, or fail permanently — the appropriate response — instead of treating every distinct cause identically because the information was discarded before it reached them.

title: What gets lost when the context window fills
description: What actually happens when a long agent session runs out of context and gets summarized or truncated — and why what's dropped is rarely what's least important.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a context window's limit does to information from earlier in a long session
Identify a symptom in a long session that indicates earlier context was lost or dropped

contentSections.title: "Didn't we already rule that out?"

contentSections.body: Ninety minutes into a long refactor session, you told the agent: "don't use the `legacy-http` client for this, it doesn't support the retry behavior we need — use `fetch-plus` instead." It agreed, and used `fetch-plus` for the next forty minutes of work. Two hours later, deep into a different part of the same session, it proposes adding a new HTTP call using `legacy-http`, with no acknowledgment that this was already discussed and ruled out. It isn't being contrary. The instruction from two hours and several thousand words of conversation ago is very possibly no longer inside whatever the model is actually attending to when it makes this new suggestion.

A context window is finite. A long session eventually produces more conversation than fits inside it, and something has to give — either older content gets dropped outright, or it gets compressed into a summary that keeps the gist and loses the specifics.
